body: ## Part One · Underground

Both the author of these notes and the Notes themselves are, of course, invented. Nevertheless, people like the writer of such notes not only may but must exist in our society, considering the circumstances under which our society in general has been formed. I wanted to bring before the public, more clearly than usual, one of the characters of the recent past. He is one of the representatives of a generation that is still living out its days. In this first part, entitled “Underground”, this person introduces himself and his view of things, and tries, as it were, to explain the reasons why he appeared and was bound to appear among us. In the second part come this person’s actual “notes” about certain events in his life. (Fyodor Dostoevsky)

I am a sick man... I am a spiteful man. An unattractive man, that’s what I am. I think there is something wrong with my liver. But then, I don’t understand a damned thing about my illness, and I don’t know for certain what is wrong with me. I am not being treated and never have been, though I respect medicine and doctors. Besides, I am superstitious in the extreme; well, at least superstitious enough to respect medicine. (I am educated enough not to be superstitious, but I am superstitious.) No, sir, I refuse to be treated out of spite. That, I expect, you will not be so good as to understand. Well, sir, I understand it. Of course, I shan’t be able to explain to you exactly whom I am getting at with my spite in this case; I know perfectly well that I can’t possibly do the doctors any harm by not being treated by them; I know better than anyone that all this will hurt only me and nobody else. But still, if I am not being treated, it is out of spite. My liver hurts: well, let it hurt even more!

I have been living like this for a long time now: about twenty years. Now I am forty. I used to be in the service, but I am not any more. I was a spiteful official. I was rude, and I enjoyed it. After all, I didn’t take bribes, so I had to reward myself somehow. (A bad joke, but I won’t cross it out. I wrote it thinking it would be very witty; and now that I see for myself that I only wanted to show off disgustingly, I won’t cross it out on purpose!) When people came up to the desk where I sat to ask for information, I used to gnash my teeth at them and feel an inexorable pleasure whenever I managed to upset someone. I almost always managed. Most of them were timid people: petitioners, you know. But among the dandies there was one officer in particular I couldn’t stand. He would not submit at any price, and he rattled his sword in a disgusting way. I waged war with him over that sword for a year and a half. In the end I won. He stopped rattling.

That happened in my youth, by the way. But do you know, gentlemen, what the main point of my spite was? Why, the whole thing, the vilest thing of all, was that every minute, even at the moment of my most violent bile, I was shamefully aware that I was not only not a spiteful man but not even an embittered one, that I was only frightening sparrows for nothing and amusing myself with it. I am foaming at the mouth, but bring me some little doll, give me a cup of tea with sugar, and I dare say I’ll calm down. I’ll even be touched to the bottom of my soul, though afterwards, no doubt, I’ll gnash my teeth at myself and suffer from insomnia for months out of shame. That’s my way.

I was lying about myself just now when I said I was a spiteful official. I lied out of spite. I was simply playing games, both with the petitioners and with the officer, and in reality I could never become spiteful. Every minute I was aware of a great, great many elements in me utterly opposed to it. I felt them simply swarming in me, these opposite elements. I knew that they had been swarming in me all my life and begging to be let out, but I would not let them out, would not, deliberately would not let them out. They tormented me to the point of shame; they drove me to convulsions, and I got sick of them at last, so sick of them! Doesn’t it seem to you, gentlemen, that I am now repenting of something before you, that I am asking your forgiveness for something?... I am sure it seems so to you... But, I assure you, it’s all the same to me if it does...

I could not become anything, not even spiteful: neither spiteful nor kind, neither a scoundrel nor an honest man, neither a hero nor an insect. And now I am living out my life in my corner, taunting myself with the spiteful and useless consolation that an intelligent man cannot seriously become anything, and that only a fool becomes something. Yes, sir, an intelligent man of the nineteenth century must be, and is morally obliged to be, a creature essentially without character; while a man of character, a man of action, is a creature essentially limited. That is my conviction of forty years. I am forty now, and forty years, you know, is a whole lifetime; it is extreme old age. To live past forty is indecent, vulgar, immoral! Who lives past forty? Answer sincerely, honestly. I’ll tell you who: fools and scoundrels. I’ll say it to the faces of all the old men, all those venerable old men, all those silver-haired and sweet-smelling old men! I’ll say it to the face of the whole world! I have the right to talk like this, because I myself will live to sixty. I’ll live to seventy! I’ll live to eighty!... Wait! Let me catch my breath...

You probably think, gentlemen, that I want to make you laugh? Wrong again. I am not at all such a cheerful fellow as you think, or as you perhaps think. However, if, irritated by all this chatter (and I can already feel that you are irritated), you take it into your heads to ask me who exactly I am, I will answer: I am a collegiate assessor. I worked in the service so as to have something to eat (but only for that), and when last year one of my distant relatives left me six thousand roubles in his will, I immediately retired and settled down in my corner. I lived in this corner before, but now I have settled down in it. My room is wretched, nasty, on the edge of the city. My servant is a peasant woman, old, spiteful out of stupidity, and she always smells bad besides. I am told that the Petersburg climate is getting bad for me, and that with my insignificant means it is very expensive to live in Petersburg. I know all that, I know it better than all those experienced and wise advisers and nodders. But I am staying in Petersburg; I will not leave Petersburg! I won’t leave because... Oh, but it’s all the same, really, whether I leave or not.
And anyway: what can a decent man talk about with the greatest pleasure?
Answer: himself.
Well then, I too will talk about myself.
## II

I want now to tell you, gentlemen, whether you want to hear it or not, why I could not even become an insect. I tell you solemnly that I wanted to become an insect many times. But I was not even worthy of that. I swear to you, gentlemen, that to be too conscious is an illness, a real, thorough illness. For everyday human life ordinary human consciousness would be more than enough: that is, half or a quarter of the portion that falls to the lot of a cultivated man of our unhappy nineteenth century, especially one who has the double misfortune of living in Petersburg, the most abstract and premeditated city on the whole globe. (There are premeditated cities and unpremeditated ones.) It would be quite enough, for example, to have the consciousness that all so-called spontaneous people and men of action live by. I bet you think I am writing all this to show off, to make witty remarks at the expense of men of action, and that I am rattling my sword in bad taste, like my officer. But, gentlemen, who can be vain of his own illnesses, and show off with them too?

But what am I saying? Everyone does that; people are vain precisely of their illnesses, and I, perhaps, more than anyone. Let’s not argue; my objection is absurd. But all the same I am firmly convinced that not only too much consciousness, but any consciousness at all, is an illness. I insist on it. Let us leave that for a moment too. Tell me this: why did it happen, as if on purpose, that at the very moments, yes, at the very same moments when I was most capable of being conscious of all the refinements of “the beautiful and the sublime”, as we used to say, I happened not merely to be conscious of, but to do, such ugly things, such things as... well, in a word, things that perhaps everyone does, but which, as if on purpose, came to me precisely when I was most conscious that they ought not to be done at all? The more conscious I was of goodness and of all that “beautiful and sublime”, the deeper I sank into my mire and the more capable I was of getting stuck in it altogether. But the main thing was that all this seemed not to be accidental in me, but as if it had to be so. As if it were my most normal condition, and not at all an illness or a vice, so that in the end I lost even the wish to fight against this vice. It ended with my almost believing (and perhaps I really did believe) that this might well be my normal condition.

But at first, at the beginning, what agonies I went through in that struggle! I did not believe that this happened to others, and so all my life I kept it to myself as a secret. I was ashamed (perhaps I am ashamed even now); I got to the point of feeling a kind of secret, abnormal, mean little pleasure in going home to my corner on some most disgusting Petersburg night and being acutely conscious that today again I had done something vile, that what was done could never be undone, and inwardly, secretly, gnawing, gnawing at myself for it, sawing at myself and sucking at myself until the bitterness turned at last into a kind of shameful, accursed sweetness, and finally into a decided, serious pleasure! Yes, into pleasure, into pleasure! I insist on it. I have started talking precisely because I keep wanting to know for certain: do other people have such pleasures?

I will explain to you: the pleasure here came precisely from too vivid a consciousness of your own humiliation; from feeling yourself that you had reached the last wall; that it is vile, but that it cannot be otherwise; that there is no way out for you, that you will never become a different person; that even if there were still time and faith enough to change into something different, you probably would not want to change yourself; and if you did want to, you still would not do anything, because in reality there is perhaps nothing to change into. And the main thing, and the end of it all, is that all this happens according to the normal and fundamental laws of heightened consciousness, and by the inertia that follows directly from those laws, and consequently not only can you not change yourself, but you simply cannot do anything at all. It follows, for example, from heightened consciousness that you are right to be a scoundrel, as if it were any consolation to a scoundrel to feel that he really is a scoundrel. But enough... Ah, I have piled up a lot of words, but what have I explained?... What explains the pleasure here? But I will explain myself! I will see it through to the end! That is why I took up my pen...

I, for example, am terribly vain. I am suspicious and touchy, like a hunchback or a dwarf; but really, there have been moments when, if someone had happened to slap my face, I might even have been glad of it. I say it seriously: I would probably have managed to find a kind of pleasure even in that; the pleasure of despair, of course, but it is in despair that the most burning pleasures occur, especially when you are very strongly conscious that your position is hopeless. And with a slap in the face, why, you are simply crushed by the consciousness of what a pulp you have been ground into. The main thing is that, however you look at it, it always turns out that I am the first to blame for everything, and, what is most humiliating, to blame without being guilty, and, so to speak, by the laws of nature. To blame, in the first place, because I am cleverer than everyone around me. (I have always considered myself cleverer than everyone around me, and sometimes, would you believe it, I have even been ashamed of it. At any rate, all my life I have somehow looked away and could never look people straight in the eye.) To blame, finally, because if there were any magnanimity in me, it would only give me more torment from the consciousness of how useless it all is. For I would certainly not have been able to do anything with my magnanimity: neither to forgive, because perhaps the offender struck me by the laws of nature, and one cannot forgive the laws of nature; nor to forget, because though they are the laws of nature, it still hurts. Finally, even if I wanted to be not magnanimous at all, but, on the contrary, wished to take revenge on the offender, I could not take revenge on anyone for anything, because I would certainly never bring myself to do anything, even if I could. Why would I not bring myself to? About that I want to say a few words separately.
## III

Take people who know how to avenge themselves and, in general, how to stand up for themselves. How do they do it? Once the feeling of revenge takes hold of them, say, there is nothing else left in their whole being for that time but that feeling. Such a gentleman charges straight at his goal like a maddened bull, horns lowered, and only a wall, perhaps, will stop him. (By the way: in front of a wall such gentlemen, that is, spontaneous people and men of action, sincerely give up. For them a wall is not an excuse, as it is for us, people who think and who therefore do nothing; not a pretext for turning back, a pretext which people like us usually don’t believe in ourselves, but which we are always very glad of. No, they give up in all sincerity. The wall has something soothing about it for them, something morally decisive and final, perhaps even something mystical... But more about the wall later.) Well, it is exactly this spontaneous man that I regard as the real, normal man, the one tender Mother Nature herself wished to see when she graciously brought him into being on earth. I envy such a man until I choke on my own bile. He is stupid, I won’t argue with you about that; but perhaps a normal man ought to be stupid, how do you know? Perhaps it is even very beautiful. And I am all the more convinced of this suspicion, so to speak, because if you take the opposite of the normal man, that is, the man of heightened consciousness, who came, of course, not out of the lap of nature but out of a laboratory flask (this is almost mysticism, gentlemen, but I suspect that too), then this test-tube man sometimes gives up so completely before his opposite that he himself, with all his heightened consciousness, honestly regards himself as a mouse and not a man. A highly conscious mouse, perhaps, but a mouse all the same, while the other is a man, and therefore... and so on. And the main thing is that he himself, he himself regards himself as a mouse; nobody asks him to; and that is an important point.

Now let us look at this mouse in action. Suppose, for example, that it too has been insulted (and it is almost always insulted) and that it too wants revenge. There may be even more spite piled up in it than in *l’homme de la nature et de la vérité*, the natural, truthful man. The nasty, low little wish to pay back the offender in kind may scratch at it even more nastily than at the natural man, because the natural man, in his inborn stupidity, regards his revenge quite simply as justice, while the mouse, because of its heightened consciousness, denies that there is any justice in it. At last it comes to the deed itself, to the very act of revenge. On top of the one original nastiness, the unhappy mouse has already managed to pile up around itself, in the form of questions and doubts, so many other nastinesses, and has hung so many unresolved questions on the one question, that whether it likes it or not a kind of fatal swill gathers around it, a stinking mess made of its doubts, its agitations and, finally, of the spit showered on it by the men of action, who stand solemnly around it like judges and dictators and laugh at it with all their healthy throats. Of course, there is nothing left for it but to wave the whole thing away with its little paw and, with a smile of pretended contempt that it doesn’t believe in itself, to slip shamefully back into its crack.

There, in its nasty, stinking underground, our insulted, beaten-down and ridiculed mouse at once sinks into a cold, venomous and, above all, everlasting spite. For forty years on end it will remember its insult down to the last, most shameful details, and each time it will add details of its own that are more shameful still, spitefully teasing and goading itself with its own imagination. It will be ashamed of its imagination, but it will still remember everything, go over everything, invent things about itself that never happened, on the pretext that they too might have happened, and it will forgive nothing. Perhaps it will even begin to take revenge, but in fits and starts, in petty ways, from behind the stove, incognito, believing neither in its right to revenge nor in the success of its revenge, and knowing in advance that from all its attempts at revenge it will suffer a hundred times more than the one it is taking revenge on, who perhaps won’t even scratch himself. On its deathbed it will remember everything again, with the interest that has piled up over all that time, and... But it is precisely in this cold, loathsome half-despair and half-belief, in this conscious burying of oneself alive out of grief, in the underground, for forty years; in this hopelessness, so carefully constructed and yet partly doubtful; in all this poison of unsatisfied desires turned inward; in all this fever of hesitations, of decisions taken forever and of regrets that come again a minute later: it is in all this that the juice of that strange pleasure I spoke of lies. It is so subtle, sometimes so hard for consciousness to grasp, that people who are even slightly limited, or simply people with strong nerves, will not understand a single feature of it. “Perhaps,” you will add with a grin, “people who have never had their faces slapped won’t understand it either,” and in this way you will politely hint that I too, perhaps, have had my face slapped in my time, and so I speak as an expert. I bet that is what you are thinking. But don’t worry, gentlemen, nobody has ever slapped my face, though it is all the same to me what you think about it. Perhaps I am even sorry that I have handed out so few slaps in my life. But enough: not another word about this subject, which you find so extremely interesting.

I will go on calmly about the people with strong nerves who do not understand a certain refinement of pleasure. Although these gentlemen, in certain circumstances, bellow like bulls at the top of their lungs, and although this, let us suppose, does them the greatest credit, yet, as I have already said, before the impossible they submit at once. The impossible means a stone wall? What stone wall? Why, the laws of nature, of course, the conclusions of the natural sciences, mathematics. Once they prove to you, for example, that you are descended from a monkey, there is no use making faces: accept it as it is. Once they prove to you that, in essence, one little drop of your own fat must be dearer to you than a hundred thousand people like you, and that in the end all so-called virtues and duties and other ravings and prejudices will be resolved by this conclusion, then just accept it; there is nothing to be done, because two times two is mathematics. Just try to object.

“Excuse me,” they will shout at you, “you can’t rebel: this is two times two makes four! Nature doesn’t ask your permission; it doesn’t care about your wishes, or whether you like its laws or not. You are obliged to accept it as it is, and therefore all its results as well. A wall, you see, is a wall... and so on and so on.” Good Lord, what do I care about the laws of nature and arithmetic, when for some reason I don’t like these laws, or two times two makes four? Of course I won’t break through such a wall with my forehead if I really don’t have the strength to break through it; but I won’t make peace with it either, just because it is a stone wall and I didn’t have the strength.

As if such a stone wall really were a comfort, and really held some word of peace for the world, simply because it is two times two makes four. Oh, absurdity of absurdities! How much better to understand everything, to be conscious of everything, all the impossibilities and stone walls; not to make peace with a single one of these impossibilities and stone walls if making peace disgusts you; to arrive, by the most inevitable logical steps, at the most revolting conclusions on the eternal theme that you are somehow to blame even for the stone wall, although once again it is perfectly obvious that you are not to blame at all; and as a result, silently and helplessly grinding your teeth, to freeze voluptuously in inertia, dreaming that it turns out there is not even anyone to be angry with; that no object can be found, and perhaps never will be; that there is a switch here, a sleight of hand, a card-sharper’s trick, that it is simply a mess: nobody knows what and nobody knows who. But in spite of all these unknowns and tricks, it still hurts you, and the more you don’t know, the more it hurts!
## IV
“Ha, ha, ha! Next you’ll be finding pleasure in toothache!” you will cry, laughing.

“Well, why not? There is pleasure in toothache too,” I will answer. “I had toothache for a whole month; I know there is. Of course, in that case people don’t rage in silence; they moan. But these are not honest moans; they are moans with malice in them, and the malice is the whole point. These moans express the sufferer’s pleasure; if he felt no pleasure in them, he wouldn’t moan. This is a good example, gentlemen, and I will develop it. What these moans express is, first, the whole pointlessness of your pain, so humiliating to our consciousness; the whole lawfulness of nature, which of course you don’t give a damn about, but which makes you suffer all the same, while it does not suffer at all. They express the awareness that no enemy is to be found, and yet the pain is there; the awareness that, for all the dentists in Petersburg, you are completely the slave of your teeth; that if someone wishes it, your teeth will stop aching, and if not, they will go on aching for another three months; and finally, that if you still don’t agree and go on protesting, all that is left for your own consolation is to whip yourself, or to beat your wall harder with your fist, and absolutely nothing else. Well, it is out of these bloody insults, out of this mockery from nobody knows whom, that the pleasure finally begins, a pleasure that sometimes reaches the height of voluptuousness. I beg you, gentlemen, listen some time to the moans of an educated man of the nineteenth century who has toothache, on the second or third day, when he is no longer moaning the way he did on the first day, that is, not simply because his teeth ache; not like some coarse peasant, but like a man touched by progress and European civilisation, a man who has ‘torn himself away from the soil and from the roots of the people’, as they put it nowadays. His moans become somehow nasty, vilely spiteful, and they go on for whole days and nights. And he knows himself that his moaning will do him no good at all; he knows better than anyone that he is only straining and irritating himself and others for nothing; he knows that even the audience he is performing for, and his whole family, have by now come to listen to him with disgust, don’t believe a word of it, and understand in their hearts that he could moan differently, more simply, without trills and flourishes, and that he is only doing it out of spite and malice. Well, it is in all these realisations and disgraces that the voluptuousness lies. ‘I am disturbing you, I am tearing at your hearts, I am keeping everyone in the house awake. Well then, stay awake; you too, feel every minute that I have toothache. I am no longer the hero to you that I wanted to seem before, just a nasty little man, a good-for-nothing. Well, so be it! I am very glad you have seen through me. You find it nasty to listen to my mean little moans? Well, let it be nasty; here, I’ll give you an even nastier trill...’ You still don’t understand, gentlemen? No, it seems you have to develop very far and become very conscious to understand all the twists of this voluptuousness. You are laughing? Delighted, sir. My jokes, gentlemen, are in bad taste, of course, uneven, muddled, full of self-distrust. But that is because I do not respect myself. Can a conscious man respect himself at all?”

Well, can a man respect himself at all, can he possibly, when he has tried to find pleasure even in the very feeling of his own humiliation? I am not saying this now out of some sugary repentance. And in general I could never stand saying, “Sorry, Papa, I won’t do it again”: not because I was incapable of saying it, but on the contrary, perhaps precisely because I was only too capable of it, and how! As if on purpose, I would land in it just when I was not to blame, not even in my dreams. That was the vilest thing of all. And then once again I would be moved to the depths of my soul, repent, shed tears and, of course, deceive myself, although I was not pretending at all. My heart somehow played dirty there... Here I could not even blame the laws of nature, although the laws of nature have constantly offended me, more than anything, all my life. It is vile to remember all this, and it was vile then too. For a minute later, it used to be, I would realise spitefully that it was all a lie, a lie, a disgusting put-on lie: all those repentances, all those tender feelings, all those vows to be reborn. And if you ask why I twisted and tormented myself like that, the answer is: because it was so very boring to sit with folded arms, so I went in for these contortions. Really, that is how it was. Watch yourselves more closely, gentlemen, and you will understand that it is so. I invented adventures for myself and made up a life, just so as to live somehow.

How many times it has happened to me, well, for example, to take offence, just like that, for no reason, on purpose; and you know yourself, of course, that you took offence for no reason, that you put it on, but you work yourself up to such a point that in the end, really, you are genuinely offended. All my life I have been drawn to pulling stunts like this, so that in the end I was no longer master of myself. Another time I wanted to fall in love by force, twice in fact. And I suffered, gentlemen, I assure you. Deep down you don’t believe that you are suffering, mockery stirs, and yet I suffer, and in a real, genuine way at that; I am jealous, I am beside myself... And all from boredom, gentlemen, all from boredom; inertia crushed me. For the direct, legitimate, immediate fruit of consciousness is inertia, that is, conscious sitting-with-folded-arms. I mentioned this earlier. I repeat, I repeat emphatically: all spontaneous people and men of action are active precisely because they are dull and limited. How to explain this? Like this: because of their limitations they take the nearest, secondary causes for first causes, and so they persuade themselves more quickly and easily than others that they have found an unshakeable foundation for what they do, and they calm down; and that is the main thing. For in order to begin to act, you must first be completely at peace, with no doubts left at all. Well, and how am I, for example, to set myself at peace? Where are my first causes for me to rest on, where are my foundations? Where will I get them from? I exercise myself in thinking, and so with me every first cause at once drags another after it that is still more first, and so on to infinity. That is precisely the essence of all consciousness and thinking. So here again it is the laws of nature. And what is the result in the end? Why, the same thing. Remember: just now I was talking about revenge. (You probably didn’t take it in.) It is said: a man takes revenge because he finds justice in it. That means he has found a first cause, he has found a foundation, namely justice. So he is at peace on all sides, and therefore he takes his revenge calmly and successfully, being convinced that he is doing an honest and just deed. But I see no justice in it, and I find no virtue in it either, and so if I do start taking revenge, it will only be out of spite. Spite, of course, could overcome everything, all my doubts, and so could serve perfectly well in place of a first cause, precisely because it is not a cause. But what am I to do if I don’t even have spite (that is where I started just now, after all)? My anger, once again because of those accursed laws of consciousness, undergoes chemical decomposition. You look, and the object evaporates, the reasons vanish into thin air, the guilty party cannot be found, the insult becomes not an insult but fate, something like toothache, for which nobody is to blame; and so once again only the same way out is left: to beat the wall harder. So you give it up with a wave of the hand, because you have not found a first cause. But try letting yourself be carried away by your feeling blindly, without reasoning, without a first cause, driving consciousness away at least for a while; hate or love, just so as not to sit with folded arms. By the day after tomorrow at the very latest you will begin to despise yourself for having knowingly fooled yourself. Result: a soap bubble, and inertia. Oh, gentlemen, perhaps the only reason I consider myself an intelligent man is that all my life I have not been able either to begin or to finish anything. All right, all right, I am a chatterbox, a harmless, irritating chatterbox, like all of us. But what is to be done if the direct and only calling of every intelligent man is chatter, that is, deliberately pouring water from one empty jug into another?
## VI

Oh, if only I did nothing simply out of laziness! Lord, how I would respect myself then. I would respect myself precisely because I would at least be capable of laziness; there would be at least one quality in me that looked positive, one I could be sure of. Question: who is he? Answer: a lazybones. Why, it would be most pleasant to hear that about oneself. It would mean I was positively defined; it would mean there was something to say about me. “A lazybones!” Why, that is a title and a calling; it is a career, sir. Don’t laugh, it is so. I would then be a member of the very best club by right, and my only occupation would be respecting myself without a break. I knew a gentleman who was proud all his life of being a connoisseur of Lafite. He considered it his positive merit and never doubted himself. He died not merely with a calm conscience but with a triumphant one, and he was entirely right. And I would have chosen a career for myself then: I would have been a lazybones and a glutton, but not a simple one; one, say, who sympathised with everything beautiful and sublime. How do you like that? I have dreamed of it for a long time. This “beautiful and sublime” has pressed hard on the back of my neck in my forty years; but that is in my forty years, while then, oh, then it would have been different! I would at once have found myself a suitable activity, namely: drinking to the health of everything beautiful and sublime. I would seize on every occasion first to shed a tear into my glass and then to drink it to everything beautiful and sublime. I would turn everything in the world into the beautiful and sublime; in the vilest, most unarguable trash I would find the beautiful and sublime. I would become as tearful as a wet sponge. An artist, for example, paints a picture in the fashionable manner of Ge. At once I drink to the health of the artist who painted it, because I love everything beautiful and sublime. An author writes a piece called *As Anyone Pleases*; at once I drink to the health of “anyone”, because I love everything “beautiful and sublime”. I will demand respect for myself for this; I will hound anyone who does not show me respect. I live in peace, I die in triumph: why, that is charming, perfectly charming! And I would grow myself such a belly, build myself such a triple chin, develop such a ruby nose, that everyone I met would say, looking at me: “Now that’s a plus! That’s something really positive!” And say what you like, gentlemen, it is very pleasant to hear remarks like that in our negative age.
## VII

But all these are golden dreams. Oh, tell me, who was it who first announced, who first proclaimed, that man does nasty things only because he does not know his real interests; and that if he were enlightened, if his eyes were opened to his real, normal interests, he would at once stop doing nasty things and at once become good and noble, because, being enlightened and understanding his real advantage, he would see his own advantage precisely in the good; and it is well known that no man can knowingly act against his own advantage; so he would, so to speak, start doing good out of necessity? Oh, the babe! Oh, the pure, innocent child! Why, first of all, when has it ever happened, in all these thousands of years, that man acted only out of his own advantage? What is to be done with the millions of facts that show how people knowingly, that is, fully understanding their real advantage, have pushed it into second place and rushed off down another road, into risk, into chance, with nobody and nothing forcing them to, but as if simply not wanting the road that had been pointed out to them; and how they stubbornly, wilfully forced their way along another road, a hard, absurd one, searching for it almost in the dark? So this stubbornness and wilfulness must really have been more pleasant to them than any advantage...

Advantage! What is advantage? And will you take it upon yourself to define exactly what human advantage consists of? What if it turns out that human advantage sometimes not only can but even must consist precisely in wishing, in some cases, for what is bad for you and not what is advantageous? And if that is so, if such a case is even possible, then the whole rule goes to dust. What do you think, does such a case ever happen? You are laughing; laugh, gentlemen, but answer me this: have human advantages been counted up absolutely correctly? Aren’t there some that not only have not fitted, but cannot fit, into any classification? After all, gentlemen, as far as I know, you took your whole register of human advantages as averages from statistical figures and the formulas of economic science. Your advantages are prosperity, wealth, freedom, peace and quiet, and so on and so on; so that a man who, for example, openly and knowingly went against this whole register would be, in your opinion, and of course in mine too, an obscurantist or completely mad, wouldn’t he?

But here is what is astonishing: how does it happen that all these statisticians, sages and lovers of the human race, when they count up human advantages, keep leaving out one advantage? They don’t even take it into account in the form in which it ought to be taken, and the whole calculation depends on that. It wouldn’t be much of a disaster: just take this advantage and add it to the list. But the trouble is precisely that this tricky advantage does not fall into any classification and does not fit on any list. I have a friend, for example... Oh, gentlemen! He is your friend too; and whose friend, whose, isn’t he? When he is getting ready to do something, this gentleman will at once set out for you, eloquently and clearly, exactly how he must act according to the laws of reason and truth. More than that: he will talk to you with excitement and passion about real, normal human interests; he will mockingly reproach the short-sighted fools who understand neither their own advantage nor the real meaning of virtue; and then, exactly a quarter of an hour later, without any sudden outside cause, but precisely because of something inside him that is stronger than all his interests, he will do something completely different; that is, he will plainly go against everything he himself was saying: against the laws of reason, against his own advantage, well, in a word, against everything... I should warn you that my friend is a collective figure, and so it is somehow hard to blame him alone. That’s just it, gentlemen: doesn’t there really exist something that is dearer to almost every man than his very best advantages? Or (so as not to break the rules of logic) isn’t there one most advantageous advantage (the very one that gets left out, the one we were just talking about), which is more important and more advantageous than all the others, and for the sake of which a man, if need be, is ready to go against all laws, that is, against reason, honour, peace, prosperity; in a word, against all these beautiful and useful things, just to reach this first and most advantageous advantage, which is dearer to him than anything?

“Well, it’s still an advantage all the same,” you interrupt me. Allow me, sir, we will get to the bottom of this; and the point is not a play on words, but that this advantage is remarkable precisely because it destroys all our classifications and constantly smashes all the systems that lovers of the human race have built for the happiness of the human race. In a word, it gets in the way of everything. But before I name this advantage for you, I want to compromise myself personally, and so I boldly declare that all these beautiful systems, all these theories of explaining to mankind its real, normal interests, so that, striving inevitably to achieve them, it would at once become good and noble, are for the time being, in my opinion, nothing but logic-chopping! Yes, sir, logic-chopping! For to assert this theory of renewing the whole human race through the system of its own advantage is, in my opinion, almost the same as... well, as asserting, for example, after Buckle, that civilisation makes man gentler, and therefore less bloodthirsty and less capable of war. By logic, it seems, that is how it comes out for him. But man is so attached to systems and abstract conclusions that he is ready to distort the truth on purpose, ready to see nothing and hear nothing, just to justify his logic. I take this example because it is such a glaring one. Just look around you: blood flows in rivers, and so merrily, as if it were champagne. There you have our whole nineteenth century, the century Buckle lived in too. There you have Napoleon, both the great one and the present one. There you have North America, the everlasting union. There you have, finally, the caricature of Schleswig-Holstein... And what is it that civilisation softens in us?

Civilisation only develops in man a greater variety of sensations and... absolutely nothing more. And through developing this variety, man may perhaps reach the point of finding pleasure in blood. That has already happened to him, after all. Have you noticed that the most refined shedders of blood have almost always been the most civilised gentlemen, to whom all those Attilas and Stenka Razins sometimes could not hold a candle? And if they don’t catch the eye as vividly as Attila and Stenka Razin, it is precisely because they are met with too often, are too ordinary, too familiar. At any rate, civilisation has made man, if not more bloodthirsty, then certainly more nastily and vilely bloodthirsty than before. Before, he saw justice in bloodshed and exterminated whoever he thought deserved it with a calm conscience; while now, although we consider bloodshed a vile thing, we still go in for this vile thing, and even more than before. Which is worse? Decide for yourselves. They say Cleopatra (forgive the example from Roman history) liked to stick gold pins into the breasts of her slave girls and took pleasure in their screams and writhing. You will say that this was in times that were, relatively speaking, barbaric; that times are barbaric now too, because (also relatively speaking) pins are still being stuck in now; that even now, although man has sometimes learned to see more clearly than in barbaric times, he is still far from having learned to act as reason and science direct him. But all the same you are perfectly sure that he will certainly learn, once certain old bad habits have quite passed away, and once common sense and science have completely re-educated human nature and pointed it in the normal direction. You are sure that then man himself will stop making mistakes of his own free will and will, so to speak, be unable, even if he wanted to, to set his will against his normal interests.

More than that: then, you say, science itself will teach man (though this is a luxury already, in my opinion) that in reality he has neither will nor caprice, and never has had, and that he himself is nothing more than something like a piano key or the stop of an organ; and that, besides, there are also the laws of nature in the world; so that everything he does is done not at all by his own wishing but by itself, according to the laws of nature. Consequently, these laws of nature only have to be discovered, and man will no longer be answerable for his actions, and life will be extremely easy for him. All human actions will then, of course, be calculated according to these laws, mathematically, like a table of logarithms up to 108,000, and entered in a calendar; or better still, certain well-meaning publications will appear, like our present encyclopaedic dictionaries, in which everything will be so precisely calculated and labelled that there will no longer be any actions or adventures in the world.

Then, and all this is what you are saying, new economic relations will arrive, all ready-made and also calculated with mathematical precision, so that in an instant every possible question will vanish, simply because every possible answer will have been supplied. Then the crystal palace will be built. Then... well, in a word, then the golden age will come flying down. Of course, there is no way to guarantee (this is me speaking now) that it won’t then be, for example, terribly boring (for what is there to do when everything has been calculated in a table?), but on the other hand everything will be extremely sensible. Of course, what won’t you think up out of boredom! Gold pins are stuck in out of boredom too, after all; but none of that would matter. What is bad (this is me speaking again) is that, for all I know, people might even be glad of gold pins then. For man is stupid, phenomenally stupid. That is, he is not stupid at all, but he is so ungrateful that you could search and not find another like him. I, for example, would not be in the least surprised if suddenly, for no reason at all, in the middle of all that future universal good sense, some gentleman should appear with an ignoble, or rather a reactionary and mocking, face, put his hands on his hips and say to us all: “Well, gentlemen, why don’t we kick all this good sense to dust, once and for all, with one kick, for the sole purpose of sending all these logarithms to the devil, so that we can live again according to our own stupid will!” That would be nothing, but what is galling is that he would certainly find followers: that is how man is made. And all this from the emptiest of reasons, which hardly seems worth mentioning: namely, that man, always and everywhere, whoever he may be, has liked to act as he wanted, and not at all as reason and advantage commanded him; and one can want against one’s own advantage, and sometimes one positively must (that is my idea). One’s own free and unfettered wanting, one’s own caprice, however wild, one’s own fancy, provoked sometimes even to the point of madness: that is the very advantage that gets left out, the most advantageous advantage, which fits no classification and which constantly sends all systems and theories flying to the devil. And where did all these sages get the idea that man needs some normal, some virtuous wanting? Why did they imagine that man must have a sensibly advantageous wanting? What man needs is only independent wanting, whatever that independence may cost and wherever it may lead. And as for wanting, the devil only knows...
## VIII

“Ha, ha, ha! But when you come down to it, wanting doesn’t even exist, if you like!” you interrupt me, laughing. “Science has already managed to dissect man so thoroughly that even now we know that wanting and so-called free will are nothing but...”

Wait, gentlemen, I was going to begin like that myself. I confess I even got frightened. I was just about to shout that, after all, the devil only knows what wanting depends on, and that perhaps we should thank God for that; but then I remembered science and... sat down. And that is when you started talking. For really, well, if one day they truly find the formula for all our wants and caprices, that is, what they depend on, by what laws exactly they arise, how exactly they spread, where they tend in such and such a case, and so on and so on, that is, a real mathematical formula, then man will perhaps at once stop wanting; indeed, he will very likely stop for certain. What pleasure is there in wanting by a table? More than that: he will at once turn from a man into an organ stop or something of the kind; for what is a man without desires, without will and without wants, if not a stop on the cylinder of a barrel organ? What do you think? Let us work out the probabilities: can it happen or not?

“Hm...” you decide, “our wants are mostly mistaken because of a mistaken view of our advantages. The reason we sometimes want pure nonsense is that, in our stupidity, we see in this nonsense the easiest way to reach some advantage we had assumed in advance. Well, and when all this has been explained and calculated on paper (which is quite possible, since it is vile and senseless to believe in advance that man will never discover certain laws of nature), then of course there will be no so-called desires any more. For if wanting ever comes completely to terms with reason, then we shall reason instead of wanting, precisely because it is impossible, for example, while keeping one’s reason, to want nonsense and so knowingly go against reason and wish oneself harm... And since all wants and reasonings really can be calculated, because one day the laws of our so-called free will are bound to be discovered, then, joking aside, something like a table really may be arranged, so that we really shall want according to this table. For if one day they calculate and prove to me, for example, that if I thumbed my nose at so-and-so, it was precisely because I could not help thumbing my nose at him, and that I had to do it with exactly that finger, then what will be left in me that is free, especially if I am an educated man who has finished a course of studies somewhere? Why, then I could calculate my whole life thirty years ahead; in a word, if this is arranged, there will be nothing left for us to do; we shall have to accept it anyway. And in general we must tirelessly repeat to ourselves that at such and such a moment and in such and such circumstances nature does not ask our permission; that we must accept her as she is and not as we imagine her; and if we really are heading towards a table and a calendar, and... well, even towards a test tube, then what can we do, we must accept the test tube too! Otherwise it will accept itself, without you...”

Yes, sir, but this is exactly where I get stuck! Gentlemen, excuse me for philosophising; it is forty years of the underground! Allow me to let my fancy run. You see, gentlemen: reason is a fine thing, that is beyond dispute; but reason is only reason and satisfies only the reasoning part of man, while wanting is the expression of the whole of life, that is, the whole of human life, reason and all the head-scratching included. And although our life, expressed this way, often turns out to be a rather trashy business, it is still life, and not just the extraction of square roots. I, for example, quite naturally want to live in order to satisfy my whole capacity for living, and not in order to satisfy only my capacity for reasoning, that is, some one-twentieth part of my whole capacity for living. What does reason know? Reason knows only what it has managed to learn (and some things it perhaps will never learn; that is no comfort, but why not say it?), while human nature acts as a whole, with everything that is in it, consciously and unconsciously, and even if it lies, it lives.

I suspect, gentlemen, that you are looking at me with pity; you repeat to me that an enlightened and developed man, in a word, the kind of man the future man will be, cannot knowingly want something that is to his disadvantage; that this is mathematics. I entirely agree: it really is mathematics. But I repeat to you for the hundredth time, there is one case, only one, when man may deliberately, consciously wish for himself something even harmful, stupid, even the stupidest thing: namely, in order to have the right to wish for himself even the stupidest thing, and not to be bound by the duty to wish only for what is clever. For this stupidest thing, this caprice of ours, may really, gentlemen, be more advantageous for people like us than anything else on earth, especially in certain cases. And in particular it may be more advantageous than all advantages even when it does us obvious harm and contradicts the soundest conclusions of our reason about advantage, because in any case it preserves for us what is most important and most precious, that is, our personality and our individuality. Some people do indeed claim that this is what is most precious of all to man. Wanting can, of course, agree with reason if it wants to, especially if one does not abuse this but uses it in moderation; that is useful and even sometimes praiseworthy. But very often, and even mostly, wanting completely and stubbornly disagrees with reason, and... and... and do you know that this too is useful, and even sometimes very praiseworthy?

Gentlemen, let us suppose that man is not stupid. (And indeed one cannot possibly say that of him, if only because, if he is stupid, then who is clever?) But even if he is not stupid, he is still monstrously ungrateful! Phenomenally ungrateful. I even think that the best definition of man is: a creature that goes on two legs and is ungrateful. But that is not all; that is not yet his chief failing. His chief failing is his constant bad behaviour, constant from the Flood to the Schleswig-Holstein period of human destiny. Bad behaviour, and therefore bad sense; for it has long been known that bad sense comes from nothing but bad behaviour. Just try casting a glance at the history of mankind; well, what will you see? Is it majestic? Majestic, perhaps; the Colossus of Rhodes alone, for example, is worth something! Not for nothing does Mr Anaevsky testify that some say it is the work of human hands, while others claim it was created by nature herself. Is it colourful? Colourful, perhaps; just sorting out the dress uniforms, military and civilian, of all ages and all peoples is worth something, and with the everyday uniforms thrown in you could break your leg; no historian could keep his feet. Is it monotonous? Well, monotonous too, perhaps: they fight and fight, they fight now, they fought before and they fought after; you must agree that this is even too monotonous. In a word, you can say anything about world history, anything that might enter the most disordered imagination. There is only one thing you cannot say: that it is sensible. You would choke on the first word.

And here is the kind of thing you come across every minute: there are always people appearing in life who are so well-behaved and so sensible, such sages and lovers of the human race, who make it their aim all their lives to behave as well and as sensibly as possible, to be a light, so to speak, to their neighbours, precisely in order to prove to them that it really is possible to live in the world both well-behaved and sensible. And what happens? It is well known that many of these lovers of mankind, sooner or later, towards the end of their lives, betrayed themselves by producing some scandalous anecdote, sometimes even of the most indecent kind. Now I ask you: what can you expect of man, a creature endowed with such strange qualities? Shower him with every earthly blessing, drown him in happiness right over his head, so that only bubbles rise to the surface of happiness, as on water; give him such economic prosperity that there is nothing left for him to do but sleep, eat gingerbread and busy himself with keeping world history going; and even then, out of sheer ingratitude, out of sheer spite, man will play you some nasty trick. He will even risk his gingerbread and deliberately want the most ruinous rubbish, the most uneconomical nonsense, solely in order to mix into all this positive good sense his own ruinous, fantastic element. It is precisely his fantastic dreams, his most vulgar stupidity, that he will want to keep, solely in order to confirm to himself (as if that were so very necessary) that people are still people and not piano keys, on which the laws of nature themselves may be playing with their own hands, but which they threaten to play so thoroughly that nobody will be able to want anything not in the calendar.

And that is not all: even if he really did turn out to be a piano key, even if this were proved to him by the natural sciences and mathematically, he would still not come to his senses, but would deliberately do something contrary, out of sheer ingratitude, simply to have his own way. And if he finds he has no means, he will invent destruction and chaos, invent all kinds of suffering, and have his own way after all! He will send a curse out over the world, and since only man can curse (that is his privilege, the chief thing that distinguishes him from the other animals), he may achieve his goal by the curse alone, that is, really convince himself that he is a man and not a piano key! If you say that all this too can be calculated by a table, chaos and darkness and curse, so that the mere possibility of calculating it in advance will stop everything and reason will win, then man will deliberately go mad for the occasion, so as to be rid of reason and have his own way! I believe in this, I answer for it, because the whole business of man, it seems, really does consist in nothing but man proving to himself every minute that he is a man and not an organ stop! Proving it even at the cost of his own skin; proving it even by living like a caveman. And after this, how can one help sinning and rejoicing that this has not happened yet, and that wanting still depends, for the time being, on the devil knows what...

You shout at me (if you still deign to shout at me) that nobody is taking away my will here; that all they are trying to do is somehow arrange things so that my will, of its own free will, coincides with my normal interests, with the laws of nature and with arithmetic.

Oh, gentlemen, what kind of will of my own will there be, when it comes down to tables and arithmetic, when there is nothing in use but two times two makes four? Two times two will make four without my will. As if that were what one’s own will is!
## IX

Gentlemen, I am joking, of course, and I know myself that my jokes are not good ones; but you cannot take everything as a joke. Perhaps I am joking through clenched teeth. Gentlemen, questions are tormenting me; answer them for me. Here you are, for example, wanting to wean man from his old habits and correct his will in accordance with the demands of science and common sense. But how do you know that man not only can but must be remade like this? What makes you conclude that human wanting so badly needs correcting? In a word, how do you know that such a correction will really bring man any advantage? And, to say it all, why are you so certainly convinced that not going against our real, normal advantages, guaranteed by the arguments of reason and arithmetic, really is always advantageous for man, and is a law for all mankind? For the time being that is only your assumption. Suppose it is a law of logic; it may not be a law of mankind at all. Perhaps you think, gentlemen, that I am mad? Allow me to explain. I agree: man is above all a creative animal, condemned to strive consciously towards a goal and to practise the art of engineering, that is, eternally and ceaselessly to build himself a road, wherever it may lead. But perhaps that is exactly why he sometimes wants to swerve aside: because he is condemned to build this road; and perhaps also because, however stupid the spontaneous man of action may be in general, it sometimes still occurs to him that the road, it turns out, almost always leads somewhere or other, and that the main thing is not where it leads, but that it should keep going, and that the well-behaved child, neglecting the art of engineering, should not give himself up to ruinous idleness, which, as everyone knows, is the mother of all vices. Man loves to create and to build roads, that is beyond dispute. But why does he also passionately love destruction and chaos? Tell me that! But about this I want to say a few words separately myself. Isn’t it perhaps because he is instinctively afraid of reaching his goal and completing the building he is creating that he loves destruction and chaos so much (for it is beyond dispute that he sometimes loves them very much; that is just how it is)? How do you know: perhaps he loves the building only from a distance and not at all close up; perhaps he only loves building it and not living in it, leaving it afterwards *aux animaux domestiques*, to the domestic animals, such as ants, sheep and so on and so on. Now ants have quite different tastes. They have one amazing building of this kind, forever indestructible: the anthill.

With the anthill the worthy ants began, and with the anthill they will surely end, which does great credit to their constancy and their positive outlook. But man is a frivolous and unseemly creature, and perhaps, like a chess player, he loves only the process of reaching the goal, and not the goal itself. And who knows (one cannot vouch for it), perhaps the whole goal on earth towards which mankind is striving lies only in this endless process of getting there, in other words, in life itself, and not really in the goal, which of course must be nothing but two times two makes four, that is, a formula; and two times two makes four, gentlemen, is no longer life, but the beginning of death. At any rate, man has always somehow been afraid of this two times two makes four, and I am afraid of it even now. Suppose man does nothing but search for this two times two makes four; he sails the oceans, he sacrifices his life in this search; but to find it, to really find it, by God, he is somehow afraid. For he feels that once he has found it, there will be nothing left to search for. Workmen, when they have finished their work, at least get their money, go to the tavern, then end up at the police station, and there is a week’s occupation for you. But where will man go? At any rate, each time he reaches such goals you notice something awkward in him. He loves getting there, but having got there, not quite; and that, of course, is terribly funny. In a word, man is made comically; there is obviously a pun in all this. But two times two makes four is still a most insufferable thing. Two times two makes four is, in my opinion, nothing but a piece of insolence, sir. Two times two makes four stands there like a fop with hands on hips, blocks your road and spits. I agree that two times two makes four is an excellent thing; but if we are going to praise everything, then two times two makes five is sometimes a very charming little thing too.

And why are you so firmly, so solemnly sure that only the normal and the positive, in a word, only well-being, is to man’s advantage? Isn’t reason mistaken about advantages? Perhaps man loves something besides well-being? Perhaps he loves suffering just as much? Perhaps suffering is exactly as much to his advantage as well-being? And man does sometimes love suffering terribly, passionately, and that is a fact. There is no need to consult world history here; ask yourself, if only you are a man and have lived at all. As for my personal opinion, to love only well-being is even somehow indecent. Whether it is good or bad, smashing something now and then is also very pleasant. I am not really standing up here for suffering, or for well-being either. I am standing up for... my caprice, and for its being guaranteed to me when I need it. Suffering, for example, is not allowed in light comedies, I know that. In the crystal palace it is unthinkable: suffering is doubt, is denial, and what kind of crystal palace is it if you can doubt it? And yet I am sure that man will never give up real suffering, that is, destruction and chaos. Suffering: why, it is the sole cause of consciousness. Though I said at the beginning that consciousness, in my view, is man’s greatest misfortune, I know that man loves it and will not exchange it for any satisfactions. Consciousness, for example, is infinitely higher than two times two. After two times two, of course, there will be nothing left, not only to do, but even to find out. All you will be able to do then is stop up your five senses and sink into contemplation. Well, with consciousness the result is the same, that is, there will also be nothing to do; but at least you can sometimes give yourself a good whipping, and that livens you up, at any rate. It may be reactionary, but it is still better than nothing.

You believe in a crystal building, forever indestructible, that is, one at which you can’t stick out your tongue on the sly or make a rude sign in your pocket. Well, and perhaps I am afraid of this building precisely because it is crystal and forever indestructible, and because you won’t be able to stick out your tongue at it even on the sly.

You see: if instead of a palace there were a henhouse, and it started to rain, I might climb into the henhouse so as not to get wet; but all the same I would not take the henhouse for a palace out of gratitude for its keeping me out of the rain. You laugh; you even say that in that case a henhouse and a mansion are all the same. Yes, I answer, if one had to live only so as not to get wet.

But what is to be done if I have taken it into my head that one does not live for that alone, and that if one is going to live at all, one should live in a mansion? That is my wanting, that is my desire. You will scrape it out of me only when you have changed my desires. Well, change them, then; tempt me with something else, give me another ideal. But in the meantime I will not take a henhouse for a palace. Let it even be that the crystal building is a fantasy, that by the laws of nature it is not supposed to exist, and that I invented it only out of my own stupidity, out of certain old irrational habits of our generation. But what do I care that it is not supposed to exist? Isn’t it all the same, if it exists in my desires, or rather exists as long as my desires exist? Perhaps you are laughing again? Laugh away; I will accept all your mockery, and still I will not say that I am full when I am hungry; still I know that I will not settle for a compromise, for an endlessly recurring zero, simply because it exists according to the laws of nature and really does exist. I will not accept as the crown of my desires a big block of flats, with apartments for poor tenants on thousand-year leases, and, just in case, a dentist’s sign out front. Destroy my desires, wipe out my ideals, show me something better, and I will follow you. You may say it isn’t worth getting involved with me; but in that case I can give you the same answer. We are reasoning seriously; and if you don’t want to honour me with your attention, I won’t bow and beg. I have my underground.

And as long as I am still alive and still want things, may my hand wither if I carry even one little brick to such a block of flats! Never mind that just now I myself rejected the crystal building for the sole reason that you would not be able to tease it with your tongue. I did not say that at all because I am so fond of sticking out my tongue. Perhaps what made me angry was only that among all your buildings there is not yet a single one at which one would not want to stick out one’s tongue. On the contrary, I would let my tongue be cut off altogether, out of sheer gratitude, if only things could be arranged so that I myself would never want to stick it out again. What do I care that it can’t be arranged, and that one has to be content with apartments? Then why am I made with such desires? Can it be that I am made this way only to reach the conclusion that my whole make-up is nothing but a swindle? Can that be the whole purpose? I don’t believe it.

But do you know what? I am convinced that people like us, from the underground, need to be kept on a short leash. Though we are capable of sitting silent in the underground for forty years, once we come out into the light and break loose, we talk and talk and talk...
## XI

The long and the short of it, gentlemen: it is better to do nothing! Better conscious inertia! And so, long live the underground! Though I said that I envy the normal man to the last drop of my bile, I don’t want to be him on the terms on which I see him (though I won’t stop envying him all the same. No, no, the underground is more advantageous in any case!). There, at least, one can... Oh, but I am lying even here! I am lying because I know myself, as surely as two times two, that it is not the underground that is better at all, but something else, something completely different, which I thirst for but can never find! To the devil with the underground!

Here is what would even be better: if I myself believed even a little of everything I have just written. I swear to you, gentlemen, that I do not believe one single word, not a single little word, of what I have just scribbled! That is, perhaps I do believe it, but at the same time, for some unknown reason, I feel and suspect that I am lying like a cobbler.
“Then why did you write all this?” you say to me.

Well, suppose I put you away for forty years with nothing to do, and then came to see you in the underground after forty years, to find out what state you had reached? Can a man really be left alone without anything to do for forty years?

“And this isn’t shameful, this isn’t humiliating!” you will perhaps say to me, shaking your heads contemptuously. “You thirst for life, yet you settle the questions of life yourself with a tangle of logic. And how tiresome, how insolent your antics are, and at the same time how frightened you are! You talk nonsense and you are pleased with it; you say insolent things, and yet you are constantly afraid of them and keep apologising. You assure us that you are afraid of nothing, and at the same time you fish for our good opinion. You assure us that you are grinding your teeth, and at the same time you crack jokes to make us laugh. You know that your witticisms are not witty, but you are obviously very pleased with their literary merit. Perhaps you really have suffered, but you have no respect at all for your own suffering. There is truth in you, but there is no purity in you; out of the pettiest vanity you carry your truth out for show, for shame, to the market... You really do want to say something, but out of fear you hide your last word, because you don’t have the resolve to say it, only a cowardly insolence. You boast of consciousness, but you only waver, because although your mind is working, your heart is darkened by corruption, and without a pure heart there can be no full, right consciousness. And how tiresome you are, how you push yourself on us, how you posture! Lies, lies and lies!”

Of course, I made up all these words of yours myself just now. That too comes from the underground. For forty years on end I listened to these words of yours through a crack. I invented them myself; after all, that was all there was to invent. No wonder I learned them by heart and they took on a literary form...

But can it be, can it really be, that you are so gullible as to imagine that I will print all this, and give it to you to read, besides? And here is another puzzle for me: why do I call you “gentlemen”, why do I address you as if you really were my readers? Confessions like the ones I intend to start setting down are not printed and are not given to others to read. At least, I don’t have that much firmness in me, and I don’t think it necessary to have it. But you see, a fancy has come into my head, and I want to carry it out, whatever it costs. Here is the thing.

There are things in every man’s memories that he does not reveal to everyone, but only to his friends. There are others that he will not reveal even to his friends, but only to himself, and even then in secret. But there are, finally, things that a man is afraid to reveal even to himself, and every decent man has piled up a good number of such things. That is, it is even like this: the more decent the man, the more of them he has. At least, I myself have only recently decided to remember some of my earlier adventures; until now I have always avoided them, even with a kind of uneasiness. But now, when I am not only remembering them but have even decided to write them down, now I want precisely to test this: can a man be completely honest at least with himself, and not be afraid of the whole truth? I will note, by the way, that Heine claims that true autobiographies are almost impossible, and that a man is sure to lie about himself. In his opinion Rousseau, for example, certainly lied about himself in his Confessions, and even lied deliberately, out of vanity. I am sure Heine is right; I understand very well how one can sometimes slander oneself with whole crimes purely out of vanity, and I even grasp very well what kind of vanity that may be. But Heine was judging a man who confessed before the public. I, however, am writing for myself alone, and I declare once and for all that if I write as if addressing readers, it is only for show, because it is easier for me to write that way. It is a form, an empty form; I shall never have any readers. I have already said so...
I do not want to be restricted by anything in editing my notes. I will not introduce any order or system. Whatever I remember, I will write down.

Well, for example: someone might seize on my words and ask me: if you really are not counting on readers, then why do you now make such agreements with yourself, and on paper too, saying that you won’t introduce order or system, that you will write down whatever you remember, and so on and so on? Why are you explaining yourself? Why are you apologising?
“Well, there you are,” I answer.

There is a whole psychology in this, however. Perhaps it is simply that I am a coward. And perhaps it is that I deliberately imagine an audience in front of me so as to behave more decently while I am writing. There may be a thousand reasons.
But here is something else: why, for what purpose exactly, do I want to write? If not for the public, then surely I could just remember everything in my head, without putting it on paper?

Quite so, sir; but on paper it will come out somehow more solemn. There is something impressive in it; I will judge myself more strictly, and the style will improve. Besides, perhaps writing things down really will bring me relief. Today, for example, one memory from long ago weighs on me especially. It came back to me clearly a few days ago, and since then it has stayed with me like an annoying tune that won’t go away. And yet I must get rid of it. I have hundreds of such memories; but from time to time one out of the hundred stands out and weighs on me. For some reason I believe that if I write it down, it will leave me. Why not try?
Finally: I am bored, and I am always doing nothing. And writing really is a kind of work. They say work makes a man good and honest. Well, here is a chance, at least.

Today it is snowing, an almost wet snow, yellow and murky. It snowed yesterday too, and a few days ago as well. I think it was because of the wet snow that I remembered the story that now won’t leave me alone. So let this be a story apropos of the wet snow.
## Part Two · Apropos of the Wet Snow

> When, out of the darkness of error,
> with a burning word of conviction
> I drew your fallen soul,
> and, full of deep torment,
> wringing your hands, you cursed
> the vice that had ensnared you;
> ...
> and suddenly, covering your face with your hands,
> full of shame and horror,
> you dissolved in tears,
> shaken, overwhelmed...
> And so on, and so on, and so on.
— from the poetry of N. A. Nekrasov

At that time I was only twenty-four. Even then my life was gloomy, disordered and lonely to the point of savagery. I had nothing to do with anyone, I even avoided talking, and I buried myself deeper and deeper in my corner. At work, in the office, I even tried not to look at anyone, and I noticed very well that my colleagues not only considered me an oddity but, as it also seemed to me, looked at me with a kind of disgust. It occurred to me: why does nobody but me feel that people look at him with disgust? One of the clerks in our office had a repulsive, badly pock-marked face, even a sort of bandit’s face. I don’t think I would have dared to look at anyone with such an indecent face. Another had a uniform so worn that there was a bad smell near him. And yet not one of these gentlemen was embarrassed, either about his clothes, or about his face, or in any moral way. Neither of them imagined that people looked at them with disgust; and even if they had imagined it, they would not have cared, as long as it was not their superiors who were looking. It is perfectly clear to me now that, because of my boundless vanity, and therefore my demands on myself, I very often looked at myself with a furious dissatisfaction that reached the point of disgust, and so in my mind I attributed my view of myself to everyone else. I hated my face, for example; I thought it vile, and I even suspected that there was something mean in its expression, and so every time I came to work I tried agonisingly to carry myself as independently as possible, so that no one would suspect me of meanness, and to express as much nobility as possible with my face. “Let it be an ugly face,” I thought, “but let it be a noble face, expressive and, above all, extremely intelligent.” But I knew for certain, and it hurt, that my face would never express all these perfections. And what was most horrible of all, I found it positively stupid. I would have been quite content with intelligence. So much so that I would even have agreed to a mean expression, if only my face were thought terribly intelligent at the same time.

Of course I hated all our clerks, from the first to the last, and despised them all, and at the same time I was somehow afraid of them. Sometimes I would suddenly even rank them above myself. It happened to me suddenly in those days: one moment I despised them, the next I ranked them above myself. A developed and decent man cannot be vain without making boundless demands on himself and without despising himself at certain moments to the point of hatred. But whether I despised them or ranked them above myself, I lowered my eyes before almost everyone I met. I even made experiments: could I bear this or that person’s gaze on me? And I was always the first to look down. This tormented me to the point of fury. I was also morbidly afraid of being ridiculous, and so I slavishly worshipped routine in everything external; I lovingly fell into the common rut and was frightened with my whole soul of any eccentricity in myself. But how could I keep it up? I was morbidly developed, as a man of our time ought to be. They, on the other hand, were all dull and as like one another as sheep in a flock. Perhaps I was the only one in the whole office who constantly felt that I was a coward and a slave; and I felt it precisely because I was developed. But I did not only feel it: it really was so. I was a coward and a slave. I say this without any embarrassment. Every decent man of our time is, and must be, a coward and a slave. That is his normal condition. I am deeply convinced of it. He is made that way and built for it. And not just at the present time, because of some chance circumstances, but in general, at all times, a decent man must be a coward and a slave. That is the law of nature for all decent people on earth. If one of them happens to show courage about something, let him not take comfort in it or get carried away by it: he will lose his nerve before something else all the same. That is the one and everlasting way out. Only donkeys and their mongrels show courage, and even they only up to a certain wall. They are not worth paying attention to, because they mean absolutely nothing.
There was one more thing that tormented me then: namely, that nobody was like me and I was like nobody. “I am one, and they are all,” I thought, and fell to brooding.
From this you can see that I was still just a boy.

The opposite happened too. Sometimes going to the office became so loathsome that many times I came home from work ill. But suddenly, for no reason at all, a phase of scepticism and indifference would set in (everything with me came in phases), and then I myself would laugh at my intolerance and squeamishness, and reproach myself for romanticism. At one moment I did not want to talk to anyone, and at another I would go so far as not only to get talking but even to think of making friends with them. All my squeamishness would suddenly vanish at once, for no reason. Who knows, perhaps I never had it at all, and it was put on, out of books? I have not settled that question to this day. Once I even became real friends with them; I began visiting their homes, playing preference, drinking vodka, talking about promotions... But here allow me to make a digression.

We Russians, generally speaking, have never had those stupid, starry-eyed German and especially French romantics, on whom nothing has any effect: let the earth crack beneath them, let all of France perish on the barricades, they stay the same, they won’t change even for the sake of decency, and they go on singing their starry-eyed songs, so to speak, to the grave, because they are fools. Here, in the Russian land, there are no fools; that is well known; that is what distinguishes us from the other, German lands. Consequently, starry-eyed natures are not found among us in their pure state. It was all those “positive” journalists and critics of ours at the time, hunting for ideal landowners and sensible uncles out of novels, and foolishly taking them for our ideal, who made up these things about our romantics, taking them to be as starry-eyed as in Germany or France.
