On the contrary, the qualities of our romantic are completely and directly opposite to the starry-eyed European kind, and not a single European yardstick fits here. (Allow me to use this word “romantic”: an old-fashioned little word, respectable, well-earned and familiar to everyone.) The qualities of our romantic are: to understand everything, to see everything, and often to see it incomparably more clearly than our most positive minds see it; not to make peace with anyone or anything, but at the same time not to turn up one’s nose at anything; to get round everything, to give way to everything, to treat everyone with tact; never to lose sight of a useful, practical aim (some little government apartment, a little pension, a little decoration); to keep this aim in view through all the enthusiasms and volumes of lyric verse, and at the same time to preserve “the beautiful and sublime” in oneself intact to the grave; and, by the way, to preserve oneself too, wrapped in cotton wool like some piece of jewellery, if only, for example, for the sake of that same “beautiful and sublime”. Our romantic is a broad man, and the foremost rogue of all our rogues, I assure you of that... even from experience. All this, of course, if the romantic is intelligent. But what am I saying! The romantic is always intelligent; I only meant to note that although we did have fool romantics, they don’t count, for the sole reason that while still in the bloom of their strength they turned completely into Germans and, the better to preserve their piece of jewellery, settled somewhere over there, mostly in Weimar or the Black Forest. I, for example, sincerely despised my work at the office, and the only reason I did not spit on it was necessity, because I sat there myself and was paid for it. And as a result, note, I did not spit on it. Our romantic will sooner go mad (which, however, happens very rarely) than spit on it, if he has no other career in view; and he is never thrown out on his ear, but at most carted off to the madhouse as “the King of Spain”, and even then only if he goes very mad. But among us only the thin little fair-haired ones go mad. A countless number of romantics, though, later rise to considerable rank. An extraordinary many-sidedness! And what a capacity for the most contradictory feelings! I was consoled by this even then, and I think the same now. That is why we have so many “broad natures” who, even in their very lowest fall, never lose their ideal; and although they won’t lift a finger for that ideal, although they are notorious robbers and thieves, still they respect their original ideal to the point of tears and are extraordinarily honest at heart. Yes, sir, only among us can the most notorious scoundrel be completely, even sublimely, honest at heart, while not ceasing in the least to be a scoundrel. I repeat: again and again our romantics turn into such businesslike rascals (I use the word “rascals” lovingly), and suddenly show such a feel for reality and such knowledge of practical matters, that their astonished superiors and the public can only click their tongues at them in amazement.

A truly astonishing many-sidedness; and God knows what it will turn into and develop into in later circumstances, and what it promises us in the future. Not bad material, sir! I am not saying this out of some ridiculous, flag-waving patriotism. But I am sure you think again that I am laughing. And who knows, perhaps the reverse: perhaps you are sure that I really do think so. In any case, gentlemen, I will consider both your opinions an honour and a special pleasure. And forgive me my digression.

Of course, I did not keep up my friendship with my colleagues; I very soon fell out with them and, because of my youthful inexperience at the time, I even stopped greeting them, as if I had cut them off. That, however, happened to me only once. In general I was always alone.

At home, first of all, I mostly read. I wanted to drown everything that was constantly boiling up inside me with sensations from outside. And the only outside sensation possible for me was reading. Reading, of course, helped a great deal: it excited me, delighted me and tormented me. But at times it bored me terribly. I still wanted to move, and suddenly I would plunge into dark, underground, nasty... not debauchery, but petty debauchery. My little passions were sharp and burning because of my constant, morbid irritability. My outbursts were hysterical, with tears and convulsions. Besides reading, there was nowhere to go; that is, there was nothing in my surroundings at that time that I could respect or that drew me. On top of that, misery boiled up; there came a hysterical thirst for contradictions and contrasts, and so I took to debauchery. I haven’t said all this now to justify myself at all... But no, I am lying! I did want to justify myself. I am making a little note of that for myself, gentlemen. I don’t want to lie. I gave my word.

I went in for debauchery alone, at night, secretly, timidly, dirtily, with a shame that never left me even in the most loathsome moments, and that in such moments even reached the point of cursing. Even then I carried the underground in my soul. I was terribly afraid of being seen somehow, of being met, of being recognised. And I went to various very dark places.

Once, passing a little tavern at night, I saw through a lighted window some gentlemen fighting with billiard cues by the billiard table, and one of them being thrown out of the window. At another time I would have felt sick at it; but at that moment such a mood came over me that I envied the gentleman who had been thrown out, and envied him so much that I even went into the tavern, into the billiard room: “Perhaps,” I thought, “I’ll get into a fight too, and they’ll throw me out of the window as well.”

I was not drunk; but what can you do? Misery can eat you up to the point of such hysteria! But nothing came of it. It turned out that I was not even capable of jumping out of a window, and I left without a fight.
An officer put me in my place there at my very first step.

I was standing by the billiard table and, without realising it, blocking the way, and he needed to get past; he took me by the shoulders and silently, without warning or explanation, moved me from the place where I was standing to another, and walked past as if he had not even noticed. I could even have forgiven a beating, but I could never forgive his moving me and so completely failing to notice me.

The devil knows what I would have given then for a real, more proper quarrel, a more decent, more, so to speak, literary one! I had been treated like a fly. This officer was very tall, well over six feet; while I am a short, scrawny man. The quarrel, however, was in my hands: I had only to protest, and of course they would have thrown me out of the window. But I thought better of it and preferred... to fade away, seething.

I left the tavern confused and agitated and went straight home, and the next day I went on with my petty debauchery still more timidly, more crushed and sadder than before, as if with tears in my eyes; but I went on all the same. Don’t think, however, that I backed down before the officer out of cowardice: I have never been a coward at heart, although in practice I have constantly lost my nerve; but wait before you laugh, there is an explanation for this; I have an explanation for everything, you may be sure.

Oh, if only this officer had been one of those who agree to fight duels! But no, he was precisely one of those gentlemen (alas, long since vanished) who preferred to act with billiard cues or, like Lieutenant Pirogov in Gogol, through the authorities. They did not fight duels, and with people like us, civilians, they would have considered a duel improper in any case; and in general they thought a duel something unthinkable, free-thinking, French, while they themselves insulted people freely enough, especially when they were over six feet tall.

I lost my nerve here not out of cowardice but out of the most boundless vanity. I was not afraid of his height, or of being painfully beaten and thrown out of the window; I really would have had enough physical courage; but I lacked moral courage. I was afraid that everyone present, from the insolent billiard marker to the last rotten, pimply little clerk with a greasy collar who was hanging about there, would not understand and would laugh at me when I protested and spoke to them in literary language. Because about a point of honour, that is, not about honour, but about a point of honour (*point d’honneur*), one cannot speak among us even now except in literary language. In ordinary language a “point of honour” is never mentioned. I was quite sure (my feel for reality, in spite of all my romanticism!) that they would all simply split their sides laughing, and that the officer would not simply, that is, not harmlessly, beat me, but would certainly kick me round the billiard table with his knee, and only then perhaps take pity and throw me out of the window. Of course, this wretched story could not end for me with that alone. Afterwards I often met this officer in the street and took good note of him. Only I don’t know whether he recognised me. Probably not; I conclude this from certain signs. But I, I looked at him with spite and hatred, and so it went on... for several years, sir! My spite even grew stronger and larger with the years. At first I quietly began to make inquiries about this officer. It was hard for me, because I knew nobody. But once someone called out his surname in the street while I was following him at a distance, as if tied to him, and so I learned his name. Another time I followed him all the way to his flat, and for ten kopecks I learned from the porter where he lived, on which floor, whether alone or with someone, and so on; in a word, everything one can learn from a porter. One morning, though I had never written anything, the idea suddenly came to me of describing this officer in an exposé, as a caricature, in the form of a story. I wrote this story with delight. I exposed him, I even slandered him; at first I disguised his name so that it could be recognised at once, but then, on mature reflection, I changed it and sent the story to *Notes of the Fatherland*. But exposés were not yet in fashion then, and my story was not printed. I was very annoyed. Sometimes my spite simply choked me. At last I decided to challenge my opponent to a duel. I composed a beautiful, charming letter to him, begging him to apologise to me, and in case of refusal hinting fairly firmly at a duel. The letter was composed in such a way that if the officer had understood even a little of “the beautiful and sublime”, he would certainly have come running to me to throw his arms round my neck and offer me his friendship. And how good that would have been! How we would have lived! How we would have lived! He would have protected me with his rank; I would have ennobled him with my culture, and, well... with ideas, and so much else might have come of it! Just imagine: by then two years had passed since he had insulted me, and my challenge was the most hideous anachronism, in spite of all the cleverness of my letter in explaining and covering up the anachronism. But, thank God (to this day I thank the Almighty with tears), I did not send my letter. It sends a shiver down my spine when I remember what might have happened if I had sent it. And suddenly... and suddenly I took my revenge in the simplest, the most brilliant way! A most luminous idea suddenly dawned on me.

Sometimes on holidays I used to go to Nevsky Prospect at about four o’clock and stroll along the sunny side. That is, I did not stroll there at all, but went through countless torments, humiliations and overflowings of bile; but that, no doubt, was just what I needed. I darted like an eel, in the most unsightly way, among the passers-by, constantly making way now for generals, now for officers of the Horse Guards and the Hussars, now for ladies; at those moments I felt convulsive pains in my heart and heat down my back at the mere thought of the wretchedness of my clothes, the wretchedness and vulgarity of my little darting figure. It was sheer torture, a constant, unbearable humiliation from the thought, which turned into a constant and direct sensation, that I was a fly in front of all these people, a nasty, obscene fly; cleverer than all of them, more developed than all of them, nobler than all of them, that goes without saying, but a fly that constantly made way for everyone, humiliated by everyone and insulted by everyone. Why I took this torment upon myself, why I went to the Nevsky, I don’t know; but I was simply drawn there at every opportunity.

Even then I was beginning to feel surges of those pleasures I spoke of in the first chapter. And after the incident with the officer I was drawn there even more strongly: it was on the Nevsky that I met him most often, and there I could admire him. He too went there mostly on holidays. Although he too turned out of the way for generals and important persons, and also wriggled like an eel among them, people like me, or even a little better than me, he simply crushed; he walked straight at them as if there were empty space in front of him, and on no account gave way. I revelled in my spite as I looked at him, and... spitefully turned aside for him every time. It tormented me that even in the street I could not be on an equal footing with him. “Why must you always be the first to turn aside?” I nagged myself, in furious hysterics, sometimes waking at three in the morning. “Why you, and not him? There’s no law about it, it isn’t written anywhere, is it? Let it be equal, as it usually is when well-mannered people meet: he gives way half, and you give way half, and you pass each other with mutual respect.” But it was not like that, and I still turned aside, while he did not even notice that I made way for him. And then a most amazing idea suddenly dawned on me. “What if,” I thought, “what if I meet him and... don’t step aside? Deliberately don’t step aside, even if I have to bump into him: how would that be?” Little by little this bold idea took such possession of me that it gave me no peace. I dreamed of it constantly, terribly, and I went to the Nevsky more often on purpose, to picture to myself even more clearly how I would do it when I did it. I was in raptures. More and more this plan seemed to me both likely and possible. “Not really pushing him, of course,” I thought, already growing kinder in advance from joy, “just not stepping aside, bumping into him, not so as to hurt very much, but just shoulder to shoulder, exactly as much as decency allows; so that as hard as he bumps me, I bump him back.” At last I was completely decided. But the preparations took a very long time. The first thing was that I needed to look more respectable while carrying it out, and to see to my clothes. “Just in case, for example, a public scene develops (and the public there is superfine: a countess walks there, Prince D. walks there, the whole literary world walks there), one must be well dressed; that impresses people, and it will put us at once, in a way, on an equal footing in the eyes of high society.” With this aim I asked for an advance on my salary and bought black gloves and a decent hat at Churkin’s. Black gloves seemed to me both more solid and more stylish than the lemon-coloured ones I had had my eye on at first. “The colour is too loud, too much as if the man wants to show off,” and I did not take the lemon ones. A good shirt, with white bone studs, I had got ready long before; but the overcoat held me up badly.

My overcoat in itself was not at all bad, and it was warm; but it was padded with cotton wool, and its collar was raccoon, which was the height of a lackey’s taste. I had to change the collar at any cost and get a beaver one, like the officers’. For this I began going round the Gostiny Dvor arcade, and after several tries I set my sights on a cheap German beaver. These German beavers wear out very quickly and soon look wretched, but at first, when they are new, they look even quite decent; and after all I needed it for only one occasion. I asked the price: it was still expensive. After thorough reflection I decided to sell my raccoon collar. The rest of the sum, which was very considerable for me, I decided to borrow from Anton Antonych Setochkin, my head of section, a meek man but a serious and positive one, who never lent money to anyone, but to whom I had once, on entering the service, been specially recommended by the important person who had got me the post. I suffered terribly. To ask Anton Antonych for money seemed to me monstrous and shameful. I even did not sleep for two or three nights; and in general I slept little then, I was feverish; my heart would sink vaguely, or suddenly begin to jump, jump, jump!.. Anton Antonych was surprised at first, then frowned, then thought it over, and lent me the money after all, taking a receipt from me entitling him to take the borrowed money out of my salary in two weeks. And so everything was ready at last; the handsome beaver reigned in place of the vile raccoon, and little by little I began to set about the business. It would not do to decide at the very first try, rashly; the thing had to be managed skilfully, precisely little by little. But I confess that after many attempts I even began to despair: we simply would not collide, and that was that! Hadn’t I prepared, hadn’t I intended? It seemed we were just about to collide, and I look, and once again I have made way, and he has passed without noticing me. I even said prayers as I approached him, asking God to fill me with resolve. Once I had quite made up my mind, but it ended only with my getting under his feet, because at the very last moment, a couple of inches away, my nerve failed. He walked calmly over me, and I bounced aside like a ball. That night I was ill again with fever and delirious. And suddenly it all ended in the best possible way. The night before, I had finally resolved not to carry out my ruinous plan and to let it all come to nothing, and with this aim I went out to the Nevsky for the last time, just to see how I would let it all come to nothing. Suddenly, three steps from my enemy, I unexpectedly made up my mind, shut my eyes, and... we bumped hard, shoulder to shoulder! I did not yield an inch and walked past on a completely equal footing! He did not even look round, and pretended not to have noticed; but he only pretended, I am sure of it. I am sure of it to this day! Of course, I got the worst of it; he was stronger; but that was not the point. The point was that I had reached my goal, kept up my dignity, not yielded a single step, and publicly put myself on an equal social footing with him. I came home completely avenged for everything. I was in raptures. I was triumphant, and I sang Italian arias. Of course, I won’t describe to you what happened to me three days later; if you have read my first part, “Underground”, you can guess for yourselves. The officer was later transferred somewhere; I haven’t seen him for about fourteen years now. How is he now, my dear fellow? Whom is he crushing?
## II

But a phase of my petty debauchery would come to an end, and I would feel terribly sick. Remorse would set in; I drove it away: it made me too sick. Little by little, however, I got used to this too. I got used to everything; that is, not exactly got used to it, but somehow voluntarily agreed to put up with it. But I had a way out that reconciled everything: escaping into “the beautiful and sublime”, in dreams, of course. I dreamed terribly; I dreamed for three months on end, huddled in my corner, and believe me, at those moments I was nothing like the gentleman who, in the panic of his chicken heart, had sewn a German beaver onto the collar of his overcoat. I suddenly became a hero. I would not even have let my six-foot lieutenant in to call on me then. I could not even picture him then. What my dreams were, and how I could be content with them, is hard to say now; but then I was content with them. In fact, I am still partly content with them now. Dreams came to me especially sweet and strong after a bout of debauchery; they came with remorse and tears, with curses and raptures. There were moments of such positive intoxication, such happiness, that I did not feel even the slightest mockery inside me, by God. There was faith, hope, love. That’s just it: I believed blindly then that by some miracle, by some outside circumstance, all this would suddenly open out and widen; that suddenly there would appear a horizon of suitable activity, beneficial, beautiful and, above all, completely ready-made (what exactly, I never knew; but the main thing was, completely ready-made), and then I would suddenly step out into God’s world, almost on a white horse and crowned with laurels. A secondary role I could not even conceive of, and that is precisely why in reality I very calmly occupied the last one. Either a hero or dirt: there was no middle. That is what ruined me, because in the dirt I consoled myself that at other times I was a hero, and the hero covered up the dirt: for an ordinary man, I told myself, it is shameful to get dirty, but a hero is too lofty to get completely dirty, and therefore one may get dirty. It is remarkable that these surges of “the beautiful and sublime” came to me even during my debauchery, and precisely when I was already at the very bottom; they came in separate little flashes, as if reminding me of themselves, but they did not destroy the debauchery by their appearance; on the contrary, they seemed to liven it up by contrast, and came in exactly the amount needed for a good sauce. The sauce here consisted of contradiction and suffering, of agonising inner analysis, and all these torments, big and small, gave a kind of piquancy, even a meaning, to my debauchery; in a word, they did the job of a good sauce perfectly. There was even a certain depth in all this. And could I have agreed to a simple, vulgar, direct, clerk’s kind of debauchery and taken all that dirt upon myself? What could there have been in it to tempt me and lure me out into the street at night? No, sir, I had a noble loophole for everything...

But how much love, Lord, how much love I used to live through in these dreams of mine, in these “escapes into the beautiful and sublime”: a fantastic love, perhaps, one that was never actually applied to anything human, but there was so much of it, this love, that afterwards, in reality, I did not even feel the need to apply it: that would have been a superfluous luxury. Everything, however, always ended most happily with a lazy and intoxicating passage into art, that is, into beautiful forms of existence, completely ready-made, heavily stolen from poets and novelists and adapted to every possible use and demand. I, for example, triumph over everyone; everyone, of course, is in the dust and forced to acknowledge all my perfections of their own free will, and I forgive them all. I fall in love, being a famous poet and a gentleman of the court; I receive countless millions and at once give them away to the human race, and right there I confess before the whole people my disgraces, which of course are not simply disgraces but contain a very great deal of “the beautiful and sublime”, something Byronic, like Manfred. Everyone weeps and kisses me (what blockheads they would be otherwise), and I go off barefoot and hungry to preach new ideas, and I rout the reactionaries at Austerlitz. Then a march is played, an amnesty is granted, the Pope agrees to leave Rome for Brazil; then there is a ball for all Italy at the Villa Borghese on the shores of Lake Como, since Lake Como has been moved to Rome specially for the occasion; then a scene in the bushes, and so on and so on; as if you didn’t know! You will say it is vulgar and mean to bring all this out to market now, after so many raptures and tears, which I myself have confessed. Why mean, sir? Do you really think I am ashamed of all this, and that it was all more stupid than anything at all in your lives, gentlemen? And besides, believe me, some of it was not at all badly put together... Not everything happened on Lake Como. But then, you are right; it really is vulgar and mean. And meanest of all is that I have now begun to justify myself to you. And meaner still is that I am making this remark now. But enough, or I shall never finish: each thing will be meaner than the last...

I was never able to dream for more than three months at a stretch, and I would begin to feel an irresistible need to plunge into society. To plunge into society meant, for me, going to visit my head of section, Anton Antonych Setochkin. He was the only steady acquaintance I have had in my whole life, and I am even surprised at this myself now. But even to him I went only when such a phase had arrived, and my dreams had reached such happiness, that I absolutely had to embrace people and all mankind at once; and for that I needed to have at least one person at hand, one who actually existed. One had to call on Anton Antonych on Tuesdays, however (his day), and so I always had to adjust my need to embrace all mankind to fit a Tuesday. This Anton Antonych lived near Five Corners, on the fourth floor, in four little rooms, low-ceilinged and each smaller than the last, with the most economical and yellowish look. He had two daughters and their aunt, who poured the tea. The daughters were thirteen and fourteen, both snub-nosed, and I was terribly embarrassed by them, because they kept whispering to each other and giggling. The master of the house usually sat in his study, on a leather sofa, at a table, with some grey-haired guest, an official from our department or even from another one. I never saw more than two or three guests there, and always the same ones. They talked about the excise, about the bidding in the Senate, about salaries, about promotions, about His Excellency, about the art of pleasing, and so on and so on. I had the patience to sit beside these people like a fool for four hours at a time and listen to them, not daring and not knowing how to talk to them about anything. I grew dull; several times I would break into a sweat; a kind of paralysis hovered over me; but it was good and useful. When I got home, I would put off my wish to embrace all mankind for a while.

I did have, however, what seemed like one more acquaintance, Simonov, a former schoolfellow of mine. I had plenty of schoolfellows in Petersburg, perhaps, but I had nothing to do with them and even stopped greeting them in the street. Perhaps I even transferred to another department so as not to be with them and to cut myself off at a stroke from my whole hateful childhood. A curse on that school, on those terrible years of penal servitude! In a word, I broke with my schoolfellows as soon as I got out into the world. There remained two or three people whom I still greeted when we met. Among them was Simonov, who had not distinguished himself in any way at school, was even-tempered and quiet; but I had noticed in him a certain independence of character and even honesty. I don’t even think he was all that limited. I once had some rather bright moments with him, but they did not last long and were somehow suddenly veiled in fog. He was evidently weighed down by these memories and seemed always afraid that I would fall into my old tone. I suspected that he found me very distasteful, but I still went to see him, not being sure of it.

And so one Thursday, unable to bear my loneliness, and knowing that on Thursdays Anton Antonych’s door was closed, I remembered Simonov. As I climbed up to his fourth floor I was thinking precisely that this gentleman found me a burden and that I was going there for nothing. But since such thoughts always ended, as if on purpose, by egging me on still more to climb into an awkward situation, I went in. It was almost a year since I had last seen Simonov.
## III

I found two more of my schoolfellows there with him. They were evidently discussing an important matter. Neither of them paid almost any attention to my arrival, which was even strange, since I had not seen them for years. Evidently they took me for something like the most ordinary fly. I had not been treated like that even at school, though everyone there hated me. I understood, of course, that they must despise me now for the failure of my career in the service, and because I had let myself go badly, went about in shabby clothes and so on, which in their eyes was the signboard of my incompetence and my small importance. But all the same I had not expected such contempt. Simonov was even surprised that I had come. He had always seemed surprised when I came, even before. All this disconcerted me; I sat down in some distress and began to listen to what they were discussing.

It was a serious and even heated conversation about a farewell dinner which these gentlemen wanted to give, all together, the very next day, to a schoolfellow of theirs, Zverkov, an army officer, who was leaving for a distant province. Monsieur Zverkov had been my schoolfellow too, all through. I had begun to hate him particularly in the upper classes. In the lower classes he had been simply a pretty, lively boy whom everyone loved. I hated him in the lower classes as well, though, precisely because he was a pretty, lively boy. He always did badly at his lessons, and the further he went, the worse he did; yet he left school successfully, because he had patrons. In his last year at our school he came into an inheritance of two hundred serfs, and since almost all of us were poor, he even began to show off in front of us. He was vulgar in the highest degree, but a good-natured fellow all the same, even when he was showing off. And among us, in spite of our outward, fantastic and high-flown forms of honour and pride, everyone except a very few fawned on Zverkov, the more he showed off. And they did not fawn out of any self-interest, but simply because he was a man favoured by the gifts of nature. Besides, it was somehow accepted among us to regard Zverkov as an expert in matters of smartness and good manners. This last particularly infuriated me. I hated the sharp, self-assured sound of his voice, his adoration of his own witticisms, which came out terribly stupid, though he was bold with his tongue; I hated his handsome but silly face (for which, by the way, I would gladly have exchanged my clever one), and his free-and-easy officer’s manners of the forties. I hated the way he talked about his future successes with women (he did not dare begin with women before he had his officer’s epaulettes, and waited for them impatiently) and about how he would be fighting duels every minute. I remember how I, always silent, suddenly locked horns with Zverkov when, talking once in free time with his friends about future pleasures and frolicking at last like a young puppy in the sun, he suddenly announced that he would not leave a single village girl on his estate untouched, that it was his *droit de seigneur*, the lord’s right; and that if the peasants dared to protest, he would have them all flogged and double the rent of every one of those bearded rascals. Our louts applauded; but I locked horns with him, not at all out of pity for the girls and their fathers, but simply because such an insect was being applauded. I won that time; but Zverkov, stupid as he was, was cheerful and bold, and so he laughed it off, and in such a way that, to tell the truth, I did not quite win after all: the laugh stayed on his side. Afterwards he got the better of me several more times, but without malice, somehow in fun, in passing, laughing. I did not answer him, spitefully and contemptuously. After we left school he made a move towards me; I did not resist much, because I was flattered; but we soon and naturally drifted apart. Then I heard of his lieutenant’s successes in the barracks, of how he went on the spree. Then came other rumours: of how he was getting on in the service. He no longer greeted me in the street, and I suspected he was afraid of compromising himself by bowing to so insignificant a person as me. I saw him once in the theatre too, in the third tier, already wearing the aiguillettes of an aide-de-camp. He was fawning and bowing before the daughters of some ancient general. In three years or so he had gone off a great deal, though he was still rather handsome and smart; he had become somehow puffy and was putting on weight; one could see that by thirty he would be completely flabby. And it was to this Zverkov, now leaving at last, that our schoolfellows wanted to give a dinner. They had kept up with him all these three years, though inwardly, I am sure, they did not consider themselves his equals.

Of Simonov’s two guests, one was Ferfichkin, a Russian of German descent, short, with a monkey’s face, a fool who made fun of everyone, my bitterest enemy since the lower classes; mean, insolent, a little braggart who acted the most touchy pride, though of course he was a coward at heart. He was one of those admirers of Zverkov who made up to him out of calculation and often borrowed money from him. Simonov’s other guest, Trudolyubov, was an unremarkable person, a tall military fellow with a cold face, fairly honest, but one who worshipped every kind of success and could talk only about promotion. He was some sort of distant relative of Zverkov’s, and this, stupid as it is to say, gave him a certain importance among us. He had always considered me a nobody; he treated me, though not quite politely, at least tolerably.
“Well, at seven roubles each,” Trudolyubov began, “there are three of us, twenty-one roubles: we can dine well. Zverkov doesn’t pay, of course.”
“Of course not, since we’re inviting him,” Simonov decided.

“Do you really think,” Ferfichkin broke in arrogantly and hotly, like an insolent footman boasting of his general master’s decorations, “do you really think Zverkov will let us pay alone? He’ll accept out of delicacy, but then he’ll stand us half a dozen bottles from his own pocket.”
“What do four of us want with half a dozen?” remarked Trudolyubov, paying attention only to the half dozen.
“So, three of us, four with Zverkov, twenty-one roubles, at the Hôtel de Paris, tomorrow at five o’clock,” Simonov concluded finally; he had been chosen to organise it.
“How do you mean, twenty-one?” I said, in some agitation and even, apparently, offended. “If you count me, it won’t be twenty-one but twenty-eight roubles.”
It seemed to me that to offer myself suddenly and so unexpectedly would even be very handsome, and that they would all be won over at once and look at me with respect.
“Do you want to come too, then?” Simonov remarked with displeasure, somehow avoiding looking at me. He knew me by heart.
It infuriated me that he knew me by heart.
“Why not, sir? I’m a schoolfellow too, I believe, and I confess I even feel hurt at being left out,” I began to splutter again.
“And where were we supposed to find you?” Ferfichkin broke in rudely.
“You were always on bad terms with Zverkov,” added Trudolyubov, frowning. But I had already seized hold of it and would not let go.

“It seems to me nobody has the right to judge that,” I retorted, with a tremor in my voice, as if heaven knows what had happened. “Perhaps that is exactly why I want to come now, because I was on bad terms with him before.”
“Well, who can understand you... these lofty notions...” Trudolyubov grinned.
“You’ll be put down,” Simonov decided, turning to me. “Tomorrow at five o’clock, at the Hôtel de Paris; don’t get it wrong.”
“And the money!” Ferfichkin began in an undertone, nodding at me to Simonov, but he stopped short, because even Simonov was embarrassed.
“That’s enough,” said Trudolyubov, getting up. “If he wants to come so badly, let him.”
“But ours is a private circle, a circle of friends,” Ferfichkin said angrily, also reaching for his hat. “It isn’t an official gathering. Perhaps we don’t want you at all...”

They left; Ferfichkin did not bow to me at all as he went, Trudolyubov barely nodded without looking. Simonov, with whom I was left alone, was in a state of vexed perplexity and looked at me strangely. He did not sit down and did not ask me to sit.
“Hm... yes... tomorrow, then. Will you pay the money now? I only ask so as to know for certain,” he muttered, embarrassed.
I flared up, but as I flared up I remembered that since time immemorial I had owed Simonov fifteen roubles, which, by the way, I had never forgotten, but had never paid either.
“You must agree, Simonov, that I couldn’t have known when I came in... and I’m very annoyed that I forgot...”
“All right, all right, it doesn’t matter. Pay tomorrow at the dinner. I only wanted to know... Please don’t...”
He broke off and began to pace the room with still greater vexation. As he paced, he began to come down on his heels and stamp harder.
“Am I keeping you?” I asked, after two minutes of silence.
“Oh no!” he said with a start. “That is, to tell the truth, yes. You see, I have to call on someone... Not far from here...” he added in an apologetic voice, somewhat ashamed.
“Oh, good heavens! Why didn’t you sa-a-ay so!” I cried, seizing my cap, with an astonishingly free-and-easy air, however, which came from heaven knows where.

“It’s not far... Just a step from here...” Simonov repeated, seeing me to the hall with a fussy air that did not suit him at all. “So tomorrow at five sharp!” he shouted after me on the stairs: he was very pleased that I was going. But I was in a fury.

“What possessed me, what possessed me to push myself forward!” I ground my teeth as I strode along the street. “And for that scoundrel, that piglet Zverkov! Of course I mustn’t go; of course, to hell with it: am I bound to, or what? I’ll write to Simonov tomorrow by the city post...”

But the reason I was furious was precisely that I knew for certain I would go; that I would go on purpose; and the more tactless, the more indecent it would be for me to go, the more surely I would go.

And there was even a positive obstacle to going: I had no money. All I had in the world was nine roubles. But seven of those had to be paid the next day to Apollon, my servant, as his month’s wages; he lived with me for seven roubles a month and fed himself.
Not to pay him was impossible, considering Apollon’s character. But of that rascal, that plague of mine, I will speak some other time.
However, I knew all the same that I would not pay him, and that I would certainly go.

That night I had the most hideous dreams. No wonder: all evening I had been oppressed by memories of the penal-servitude years of my school life, and I could not shake them off. I had been shoved into that school by distant relatives on whom I depended and of whom I have heard nothing since: shoved in, an orphan, already crushed by their reproaches, already brooding, silent, glaring wildly at everything. My schoolfellows met me with spiteful and merciless jeers because I was not like any of them. But I could not stand jeers; I could not get along with them as cheaply as they got along with each other. I hated them at once and shut myself away from everyone in a timid, wounded and boundless pride. Their coarseness revolted me. They laughed cynically at my face, at my clumsy figure; and yet what stupid faces they had themselves! In our school, faces somehow became especially stupid and degenerate. How many good-looking children came to us! A few years later it was disgusting even to look at them. Even at sixteen I wondered at them gloomily; even then I was amazed at the pettiness of their thinking, the stupidity of their occupations, their games, their conversations. They did not understand such essential things; they took no interest in such inspiring, striking subjects, that I could not help considering them beneath me. It was not wounded vanity that drove me to this, and for God’s sake do not come at me with those official objections that have become sickeningly stale: “that I was only dreaming, while they already understood real life even then.” They understood nothing, no real life at all, and I swear that was what revolted me most in them. On the contrary, they took the most obvious, glaring reality in a fantastically stupid way, and even then they had got used to worshipping nothing but success. Everything that was just, but humiliated and downtrodden, they laughed at cruelly and shamefully. They took rank for intelligence; at sixteen they were already talking about cushy jobs. Of course, much of this came from stupidity, from the bad example that had surrounded them all through their childhood and boyhood. They were depraved to the point of deformity. Of course, there was more outward show in this too, more put-on cynicism; of course, youth and a certain freshness gleamed in them even through the depravity; but even their freshness was unattractive, and showed itself in a kind of smutty buffoonery. I hated them terribly, though perhaps I was worse than they were. They paid me back in the same coin and did not hide their loathing for me. But I no longer wanted their love; on the contrary, I constantly longed for their humiliation. To rid myself of their jeers, I deliberately began to study as hard as I could and forced my way to the very top of the class. That impressed them. Besides, they all began little by little to understand that I was already reading books they could not read, and understood things (not part of our special course) of which they had never even heard. They looked at this wildly and mockingly, but they submitted morally, all the more because even the teachers paid attention to me on this account. The jeering stopped, but the hostility remained, and cold, strained relations set in. In the end I could not stand it myself: with the years a need for people, for friends, developed in me. I tried to become close to some of them; but the closeness always came out unnatural and so ended of its own accord. Once I even had a friend. But I was already a despot at heart; I wanted unlimited power over his soul; I wanted to instil in him contempt for the world around him; I demanded that he break with that world, haughtily and finally. I frightened him with my passionate friendship; I reduced him to tears, to convulsions; he was a naive and devoted soul; but when he had given himself to me entirely, I at once hated him and pushed him away, as if I had needed him only to win a victory over him, only for his submission. But I could not conquer them all; my friend too was unlike any of them and was a very rare exception. My first act on leaving school was to give up the special service for which I had been intended, so as to break all the threads, curse the past and scatter its dust... And the devil knows why, after that, I dragged myself to this Simonov!..

In the morning I leapt out of bed early, jumped up in excitement, as if it were all going to begin happening at once. But I believed that some radical turning point in my life was coming, and would certainly come that very day. Perhaps because I was not used to it, all my life, at every external event, however trivial, it always seemed to me that now some radical turning point in my life was about to come. I went to the office as usual, however, but slipped away home two hours early to get ready. The main thing, I thought, is not to arrive first, or they will think I am too delighted. But there were thousands of such main things, and they all agitated me to the point of exhaustion. I cleaned my boots once more with my own hands; Apollon would not have cleaned them twice a day for anything in the world, considering it improper. I cleaned them having stolen the brushes from the hall, so that he would not notice and despise me afterwards. Then I examined my clothes in detail and found that everything was old, threadbare and worn out. I had let myself go too much. My uniform, perhaps, was in good order, but one could hardly go to dinner in uniform. And the main thing was that on my trousers, right on the knee, there was a huge yellow stain. I had a presentiment that this stain alone would rob me of nine-tenths of my dignity. I knew too that it was very low to think like this. “But this is no time for thinking; now reality is coming,” I thought, and lost heart. I knew perfectly well, even then, that I was monstrously exaggerating all these facts; but what could I do? I could no longer control myself, and I was shaking with fever. With despair I pictured how coldly and haughtily that “scoundrel” Zverkov would receive me; with what dull, irresistible contempt that blockhead Trudolyubov would look at me; how nastily and insolently that insect Ferfichkin would snigger at my expense to curry favour with Zverkov; how perfectly Simonov would understand all this to himself, and how he would despise me for the baseness of my vanity and cowardice; and, above all, how wretched, unliterary and commonplace it would all be. Of course, it would be best of all not to go. But that was the most impossible thing of all: once I began to be drawn into something, I was drawn in completely, head first. I would have taunted myself all my life afterwards: “So, you lost your nerve, lost your nerve before reality, lost your nerve!” On the contrary, I passionately wanted to prove to all that “rabble” that I was not at all the coward I imagined myself to be. More than that: in the most violent paroxysm of cowardly fever, I dreamed of getting the upper hand, of conquering them, carrying them away, making them love me, well, “for the loftiness of my thoughts and my undoubted wit”, say. They would abandon Zverkov; he would sit to one side, silent and ashamed, and I would crush Zverkov. Then perhaps I would make it up with him and drink to our friendship; but what was most spiteful and galling to me was that I knew even then, knew fully and for certain, that I did not really need any of this, that I did not really want to crush them, conquer them or win them over at all, and that for the whole result, even if I achieved it, I myself would be the first not to give a kopeck. Oh, how I prayed to God for the day to pass quickly! In inexpressible anguish I went to the window, opened the little pane, and peered into the murky haze of the thickly falling wet snow...

At last my wretched little wall clock wheezed out five. I seized my hat and, trying not to look at Apollon, who had been waiting since morning for me to pay his wages but out of pride would not speak first, I slipped past him out of the door and, in a smart cab which I had hired on purpose with my last half-rouble, I drove up like a gentleman to the Hôtel de Paris.
## IV
I had known the evening before that I would arrive first. But it was no longer a question of being first.

Not only was none of them there, but I could hardly even find our room. The table was not yet fully laid. What did it mean? After many questions I finally got the waiters to tell me that the dinner had been ordered for six o’clock, not five. The bar confirmed it. I was even ashamed to keep asking. It was only twenty-five past five. If they had changed the time, they ought at least to have let me know; that is what the city post is for; instead of exposing me to “disgrace” in my own eyes and... and even in front of the waiters. I sat down; a waiter began laying the table; with him there it felt somehow even more humiliating. Towards six o’clock candles were brought into the room, in addition to the lamps that were burning. The waiter had not thought, however, of bringing them as soon as I arrived. In the next room two gloomy diners, angry-looking and silent, were dining at separate tables. In one of the far rooms there was a great deal of noise, even shouting; one could hear the laughter of a whole gang of people, and some nasty French shrieks: it was a dinner with ladies. In a word, it was thoroughly sickening. I have rarely spent a nastier time, so that when they all appeared together at exactly six o’clock, I was glad to see them at first, as if they were some kind of liberators, and almost forgot that I was obliged to look offended.

Zverkov came in ahead of the others, evidently leading them. He and all of them were laughing; but on seeing me Zverkov drew himself up, came over unhurriedly, bending a little at the waist as if flirting, and gave me his hand, kindly but not too kindly, with a kind of cautious, almost general-like courtesy, as if, in giving me his hand, he were protecting himself from something. I had imagined, on the contrary, that as soon as he came in he would laugh his old thin, squealing laugh, and that his flat jokes and witticisms would start with the very first words. I had been preparing for them since the evening before, but I had never expected such condescension, such high-ranking affability. So he now considered himself immeasurably superior to me in every respect? If he only meant to insult me with this general’s manner, that would be nothing, I thought; I would spit it back somehow. But what if, without any wish to insult me, the little idea had seriously crept into his sheep’s head that he was immeasurably superior to me and could only look at me with patronage? The mere supposition made me choke.

“I was surprised to hear of your wish to join us,” he began, lisping and drawling his words, which he had never done before. “We never seem to meet, you and I. You avoid us. You shouldn’t. We are not as terrible as you think. Well, at any rate, I am glad to re-new our ac-quain-tance...”
And he turned carelessly to put his hat on the window sill.
“Have you been waiting long?” asked Trudolyubov.
“I arrived at exactly five o’clock, as I was told yesterday,” I answered loudly, with an irritation that promised an explosion soon.
“Didn’t you let him know we changed the time?” Trudolyubov turned to Simonov.
“No, I didn’t. I forgot,” he answered, without the least remorse, and without even apologising to me he went off to see about the hors d’oeuvres.

“So you’ve been here an hour already, oh, poor fellow!” cried Zverkov mockingly, because by his notions this really must have been terribly funny. That scoundrel Ferfichkin burst out laughing after him in his nasty little voice, ringing like a puppy’s. He too thought my position very funny and embarrassing.
“It isn’t funny at all!” I shouted at Ferfichkin, more and more irritated. “It was other people’s fault, not mine. They neglected to tell me. It’s, it’s, it’s simply absurd.”
“Not only absurd, but something else besides,” grumbled Trudolyubov, naively taking my side. “You are too mild. It was simply rude. Not on purpose, of course. And how could Simonov... hm!”
“If anyone had played a trick like that on me,” remarked Ferfichkin, “I would...”
“But you should have ordered something for yourself,” Zverkov interrupted, “or simply asked for dinner without waiting.”
“You must agree that I could have done that without anyone’s permission,” I snapped. “If I waited, then...”

“Let’s sit down, gentlemen,” cried Simonov, coming in. “Everything’s ready; I answer for the champagne, it’s perfectly chilled... I didn’t know your address; where was I to look for you?” he suddenly turned to me, but again somehow without looking at me. He evidently had something against me. He must have thought it over after yesterday.
Everyone sat down; I sat down too. The table was round. Trudolyubov was on my left, Simonov on my right. Zverkov sat opposite; Ferfichkin next to him, between him and Trudolyubov.

“Te-e-ll me, are you... in a government department?” Zverkov went on attending to me. Seeing that I was embarrassed, he seriously imagined that I needed to be treated kindly and, so to speak, encouraged. “What does he want, for me to throw a bottle at him?” I thought in a fury. Not being used to it, I was growing irritated unnaturally fast.
“In the ... office,” I answered abruptly, looking at my plate.
“And... is it pro-profitable for you? Te-ell me, what in-du-uced you to leave your former service?”

“What in-du-uced me was that I wanted to leave my former service,” I drawled three times as long, almost losing control of myself. Ferfichkin snorted. Simonov looked at me ironically; Trudolyubov stopped eating and began to examine me with curiosity.
Zverkov winced, but did not want to notice.
“We-e-ll, and what about your remuneration?”
“What remuneration?”
“I mean, your s-salary?”
“Why are you cross-examining me?”
However, I immediately told him what salary I received. I blushed terribly.
“Not much,” Zverkov remarked gravely.
“Yes, sir, you can’t dine in cafés and restaurants on that!” Ferfichkin added insolently.
“In my opinion it’s simply poor,” Trudolyubov remarked seriously.
“And how thin you’ve grown, how you’ve changed... since those days...” Zverkov added, now not without venom, with a kind of insolent pity, examining me and my clothes.
“Oh, stop embarrassing him,” cried Ferfichkin, giggling.

“My dear sir, let me tell you that I am not embarrassed,” I burst out at last. “Do you hear, sir! I am dining here, ‘in a café-restaurant’, on my own money, my own, and not other people’s, note that, Monsieur Ferfichkin.”
“Wha-at! Who here isn’t dining on his own money? You seem to be...” Ferfichkin fastened on to it, turning red as a lobster and looking me furiously in the eye.
“Just so,” I answered, feeling that I had gone too far, “and I suggest that we would do better to talk about something more intelligent.”
“You intend to show off your intelligence, I suppose?”
“Don’t worry, that would be quite superfluous here.”
“What are you clucking about, my dear sir, eh? Have you gone off your head in your de-part-ment?”
“Enough, gentlemen, enough!” Zverkov cried commandingly.
“How stupid this is!” grumbled Simonov.

“It really is stupid. We have gathered as friends to see off a good comrade on his journey, and you are settling scores,” said Trudolyubov, addressing me alone, rudely. “You invited yourself yesterday; don’t spoil the general harmony...”
“Enough, enough,” Zverkov shouted. “Stop it, gentlemen; this won’t do. Let me tell you instead how I nearly got married the day before yesterday...”

And there began some lampoon about how this gentleman had nearly got married the day before yesterday. There was not a word about marriage in it, though; but generals, colonels and even gentlemen of the bedchamber kept flashing through the story, with Zverkov almost at their head. Approving laughter began; Ferfichkin even squealed.
They all abandoned me, and I sat crushed and annihilated.

“Lord, is this the company for me?” I thought. “And what a fool I have made of myself in front of them! I let Ferfichkin go too far, though. The blockheads think they have done me an honour by giving me a place at their table, when they don’t understand that it is I, I who am doing them an honour, and not they me! ‘Thin! Clothes!’ Oh, those damned trousers! Zverkov noticed the yellow stain on the knee just now... But what does it matter! I must get up from the table at once, this very minute, take my hat and simply leave without a word... Out of contempt! And tomorrow, a duel if necessary. Scoundrels. It isn’t as if I grudged the seven roubles. They may think... Damn it! I don’t grudge the seven roubles! I’m leaving this minute!..”
Of course, I stayed.

From misery I drank Lafite and sherry by the glassful. Not being used to it, I quickly got drunk, and as I got drunk my vexation grew. I suddenly wanted to insult them all in the most insolent way and then leave. To seize the moment and show what I was: let them say, “He may be ridiculous, but he’s clever...” and... and... in a word, to hell with them!

I looked round at them all insolently with bleary eyes. But they seemed to have forgotten me entirely. They were noisy, loud and cheerful. Zverkov was doing all the talking. I began to listen. Zverkov was telling about some magnificent lady whom he had at last brought to the point of a declaration (he was lying like a horse, of course), and how in this affair he had been particularly helped by an intimate friend of his, some little prince, Kolya, a hussar, who owned three thousand serfs.
“And yet this Kolya with his three thousand serfs isn’t here to see you off,” I suddenly broke into the conversation. For a moment everyone fell silent.

“You’re drunk already,” Trudolyubov finally condescended to notice me, glancing contemptuously in my direction. Zverkov examined me in silence, like an insect. I lowered my eyes. Simonov hurriedly began pouring the champagne.
Trudolyubov raised his glass, and everyone after him, except me.
“Your health, and a good journey!” he cried to Zverkov. “To old times, gentlemen, to our future, hurrah!”
They all drank, and climbed over to kiss Zverkov. I did not move; my full glass stood untouched in front of me.
“Aren’t you going to drink?” roared Trudolyubov, losing patience and turning to me menacingly.
“I want to make a speech of my own, separately... and then I’ll drink, Mr Trudolyubov.”
“Nasty little spitfire!” grumbled Simonov.
I sat up straight in my chair and took my glass feverishly, preparing for something extraordinary, and not yet knowing myself exactly what I would say.
“*Silence!*” cried Ferfichkin. “Now we’ll hear some wit!” Zverkov waited very seriously, understanding what was coming.
“Lieutenant Zverkov,” I began, “let me tell you that I hate phrases, phrase-mongers and tight-laced waists... That is the first point, and the second will follow.”
Everyone stirred violently.
“The second point: I hate womanising and womanisers. Especially womanisers!

“The third point: I love truth, sincerity and honesty,” I went on almost mechanically, because I was already beginning to freeze with horror, not understanding how I could be talking like this... “I love thought, Monsieur Zverkov; I love true comradeship, on an equal footing, and not... hm... I love... But then, why not? I too will drink your health, Monsieur Zverkov. Seduce the Circassian girls, shoot the enemies of the fatherland, and... and... Your health, Monsieur Zverkov!”
Zverkov rose from his chair, bowed to me, and said:
“I am very much obliged to you.”
He was terribly offended, and had even turned pale.
“Damn it,” roared Trudolyubov, banging the table with his fist.
“No, sir, for that you get punched in the face!” squealed Ferfichkin.
“He should be thrown out!” grumbled Simonov.
“Not a word, gentlemen, not a gesture!” Zverkov cried solemnly, checking the general indignation. “I thank you all, but I can show him myself how much I value his words.”
“Mr Ferfichkin, tomorrow you will give me satisfaction for what you have just said!” I said loudly, turning to Ferfichkin with dignity.

“A duel, you mean? By all means,” he answered; but I must have been so ridiculous in issuing the challenge, and it suited my figure so badly, that they all, and Ferfichkin after them, simply collapsed with laughter.
“Yes, of course, leave him alone! He’s completely drunk!” said Trudolyubov with disgust.
“I’ll never forgive myself for putting him down!” grumbled Simonov again.
“Now is the moment to throw a bottle at them all,” I thought; I took a bottle and... poured myself a full glass.

“No, better to sit it out to the end!” I went on thinking. “You would be glad, gentlemen, if I left. Not for anything. I shall sit here and drink to the end on purpose, as a sign that I don’t attach the slightest importance to you. I shall sit and drink, because this is a tavern and I have paid my entrance money. I shall sit and drink, because I regard you as pawns, pawns that don’t exist. I shall sit and drink... and sing if I like, yes, sir, and sing, because I have the right... to sing... hm.”

But I did not sing. I only tried not to look at any of them; I assumed the most independent poses and waited impatiently for them to speak to me first. But, alas, they did not speak. And how, how I wished at that moment to make it up with them! It struck eight, at last nine. They moved from the table to the sofa. Zverkov stretched out on a couch, with one foot on a little round table. The wine was moved there too. He really did stand them three bottles of his own. He did not invite me, of course. They all sat round him on the sofa. They listened to him almost with reverence. It was clear that they loved him. “What for? What for?” I thought to myself. Now and then they fell into drunken raptures and kissed each other. They talked about the Caucasus, about what true passion is, about card games, about profitable posts in the service; about how much income the hussar Podkharzhevsky had, whom none of them knew personally, and they were glad he had a big income; about the extraordinary beauty and grace of Princess D., whom none of them had ever seen either; until at last they got to Shakespeare being immortal.

I smiled contemptuously and walked up and down on the other side of the room, right opposite the sofa, along the wall, from the table to the stove and back. I wanted with all my strength to show that I could do without them; and yet I deliberately stamped my boots, coming down on my heels. But it was all in vain. They paid no attention. I had the patience to walk like this, right in front of them, from eight o’clock until eleven, always over the same stretch, from the table to the stove and from the stove back to the table. “I’m walking, and no one can stop me.” The waiter coming into the room stopped several times to look at me; my head spun from turning so often; at moments it seemed to me I was delirious. In those three hours I broke into a sweat three times and dried off again. At times, with the deepest and most venomous pain, the thought pierced my heart: that ten years would pass, twenty years, forty years, and still, even after forty years, I would remember with disgust and humiliation these filthiest, most ridiculous and most terrible minutes of my whole life. It was impossible to humiliate oneself more shamelessly and more voluntarily, and I understood that fully, fully, and still I went on walking from the table to the stove and back. “Oh, if you only knew what feelings and thoughts I am capable of, and how cultured I am!” I thought at moments, mentally addressing the sofa where my enemies sat. But my enemies behaved as if I were not in the room at all. Once, only once, they turned to me, precisely when Zverkov began talking about Shakespeare and I suddenly laughed contemptuously. I snorted so affectedly and nastily that they all broke off their conversation at once and silently watched for about two minutes, seriously, without laughing, as I walked along the wall from the table to the stove, paying no attention to them whatever. But nothing came of it: they did not speak to me, and after two minutes they abandoned me again. It struck eleven.
“Gentlemen,” cried Zverkov, rising from the sofa, “now let’s all go *there*.”
“Of course, of course!” said the others.

I turned sharply to Zverkov. I was so worn out, so broken, that I would have cut my throat just to put an end to it! I was feverish; my hair, soaked with sweat, had dried and stuck to my forehead and temples.
“Zverkov! I beg your pardon,” I said sharply and decisively. “Ferfichkin, yours too, everyone’s, everyone’s; I have insulted everyone!”
“Aha! So a duel isn’t to his taste!” Ferfichkin hissed venomously.
That cut me painfully to the heart.

“No, I am not afraid of a duel, Ferfichkin! I am ready to fight you tomorrow, even after we have made peace. I even insist on it, and you cannot refuse me. I want to prove to you that I am not afraid of a duel. You will fire first, and I will fire into the air.”
“He’s amusing himself,” remarked Simonov.
“He’s simply gone soft in the head!” responded Trudolyubov.
“Let me pass; why are you standing in the way!.. Well, what do you want?” Zverkov answered contemptuously. They were all flushed; all their eyes were shining: they had drunk a lot.
“I ask for your friendship, Zverkov; I insulted you, but...”
“Insulted me? Y-you! M-me! Let me tell you, my dear sir, that you could never, under any circumstances, insult me!”
“And that’s enough of you; out of the way!” Trudolyubov added. “Let’s go.”
“Olympia is mine, gentlemen; that’s agreed!” cried Zverkov.
“We won’t dispute it! We won’t dispute it!” they answered, laughing.
I stood there, spat upon. The gang left the room noisily; Trudolyubov struck up some stupid song. Simonov stayed behind for a tiny moment to tip the waiters. I suddenly went up to him.
“Simonov! Give me six roubles!” I said decisively and desperately.
He looked at me with extreme astonishment, with somehow dull eyes. He was drunk too.
“Are you really coming with us *there* too?”
“Yes!”
“I have no money!” he snapped, grinned contemptuously, and went out of the room.
I seized him by his overcoat. It was a nightmare.

“Simonov! I saw you had money; why do you refuse me? Am I a scoundrel? Be careful how you refuse me: if you knew, if you knew why I am asking! Everything depends on it, my whole future, all my plans...”
Simonov took out the money and almost threw it at me.
“Take it, if you are so shameless!” he said mercilessly, and ran off to catch up with them.

I was left alone for a minute. Disorder, scraps of food, a broken wineglass on the floor, spilt wine, cigarette ends, drink and delirium in my head, an agonising anguish in my heart, and, finally, the waiter, who had seen everything and heard everything and was looking curiously into my eyes.
“*There!*” I cried. “Either they will all be on their knees, embracing my feet and begging for my friendship, or... or I will slap Zverkov’s face!”
“So this is it, so this is it at last, the clash with reality,” I muttered, rushing headlong down the stairs. “This is no Pope leaving Rome for Brazil, it seems; this is no ball on Lake Como!”
“You are a scoundrel,” flashed through my head, “if you can laugh at this now.”
“So be it!” I shouted, answering myself. “Everything is lost now anyway!”
They had vanished without a trace; but no matter: I knew where they had gone.

At the entrance stood a solitary night cabby, a poor one, in a coarse peasant coat, all powdered with the wet and, as it seemed, warm snow that was still falling. It was steamy and close. His little shaggy, piebald nag was all powdered with snow too, and coughing; I remember that very well. I rushed for the bast-matted sledge; but as soon as I raised my foot to get in, the memory of how Simonov had just given me six roubles knocked my legs from under me, and I collapsed into the sledge like a sack.
“No! Much must be done to redeem all this!” I shouted. “But I will redeem it, or perish on the spot this very night. Drive on!”
We set off. A whole whirlwind was spinning in my head.

“They won’t go down on their knees and beg for my friendship. That is a mirage, a vulgar mirage, disgusting, romantic and fantastic: the same ball on Lake Como. And so I must slap Zverkov’s face! I am obliged to. So it is decided; I am flying now to slap his face.”
“Faster!”
The cabby tugged at the reins.

“As soon as I go in, I’ll slap him. Should I say a few words before the slap, by way of preface? No! I’ll simply go in and slap him. They will all be sitting in the drawing room, and he on the sofa with Olympia. Damned Olympia! She once laughed at my face and refused me. I’ll drag Olympia by the hair, and Zverkov by the ears! No, better by one ear, and I’ll lead him by the ear all round the room. Perhaps they will all start beating me and throw me out. That is even certain. So be it! All the same, I will have given the slap first: the initiative is mine; and by the laws of honour that is everything; he is branded already, and no beating can wash the slap off him, only a duel. He will have to fight. And let them beat me now. Let them, the ungrateful wretches! Trudolyubov will beat me hardest: he is so strong. Ferfichkin will hang on from the side, and certainly by my hair. But let them, let them! That is what I came for. Their sheep’s heads will be forced at last to grasp the tragedy in all this! When they drag me to the door, I will shout to them that in reality they are not worth my little finger.”
“Faster, driver, faster!” I shouted at the cabby.
He even started and cracked his whip. I had shouted very wildly.

“We fight at dawn; that is decided. The office is finished. Ferfichkin said ‘de-part-ment’ just now, mocking me. But where do I get pistols? Nonsense! I’ll get an advance on my salary and buy them. And powder, and bullets? That’s the second’s business. And how can it all be done by dawn? And where will I find a second? I have no acquaintances...”
“Nonsense!” I shouted, whirling myself up still more. “Nonsense!

“The first person I meet in the street whom I ask is obliged to be my second, just as he would be obliged to pull a drowning man out of the water. The most eccentric cases must be allowed. Why, if I were to ask the director himself to be my second tomorrow, even he would have to agree, from a sense of chivalry alone, and keep it secret! Anton Antonych...”
The fact is that at that very moment the whole vile absurdity of my plans, and the other side of the coin, was clearer and more vivid to me than to anyone else in the whole world, but...
“Faster, driver, faster, you rascal, faster!”
“Ech, master!” said the voice of the people.
A sudden chill came over me.

“Wouldn’t it be better... wouldn’t it be better... to go straight home now? Oh my God! Why, why did I offer myself for this dinner yesterday! But no, it’s impossible! And the three hours’ walk from the table to the stove? No, they, and no one else, must pay me for that walk! They must wash away this dishonour!”
“Faster!”

“And what if they hand me over to the police? They won’t dare! They’ll be afraid of a scandal. And what if Zverkov refuses the duel out of contempt? That is even certain; but then I’ll show them... I’ll rush to the posting station tomorrow when he is leaving; I’ll seize him by the leg; I’ll tear his coat off him as he climbs into the carriage. I’ll sink my teeth into his hand; I’ll bite him. ‘Look, all of you, what a desperate man can be driven to!’ Let him beat me on the head, and all of them from behind. I’ll shout to the whole public: ‘Look, here is a young puppy going off to captivate the Circassian girls with my spit on his face!’

“Of course, after that everything is finished! The office has vanished from the face of the earth. They’ll seize me, they’ll try me, they’ll dismiss me from the service, put me in prison, send me to Siberia, to a settlement. No matter! Fifteen years later, when they let me out of prison, I’ll drag myself after him in rags, a beggar. I’ll find him somewhere in a provincial town. He’ll be married and happy. He’ll have a grown-up daughter... I’ll say: ‘Look, monster, look at my sunken cheeks and my rags! I have lost everything, my career, my happiness, art, science, the woman I loved, and all because of you. Here are pistols. I have come to fire my pistol and... and I forgive you.’ And then I’ll fire into the air, and nothing more will ever be heard of me...”

I even began to cry, though I knew perfectly well at that very moment that all this came from Pushkin’s *Silvio* and Lermontov’s *Masquerade*. And suddenly I felt terribly ashamed, so ashamed that I stopped the horse, got out of the sledge and stood in the snow in the middle of the street. The cabby looked at me in amazement, sighing.
What was I to do? I could not go there: it would be nonsense; and I could not leave it at that, because then it would come out... Lord! How could I leave it at that! And after such insults!
“No!” I cried, throwing myself into the sledge again. “It is predestined, it is fate! Faster, faster, there!”
And in my impatience I hit the cabby on the neck with my fist.
“Hey, what’s that for, why are you hitting me?” cried the little peasant, but he whipped up his nag all the same, so that it began kicking with its hind legs.

The wet snow was falling in flakes; I unbuttoned my coat; I did not care about it. I forgot everything else, because I had finally decided on the slap and felt with horror that it was certain to happen now, at once, and that no power on earth could stop it. The deserted street lamps flickered gloomily in the snowy haze, like torches at a funeral. The snow had got under my overcoat, under my jacket, under my tie, and was melting there; I did not cover myself up: everything was lost anyway! At last we arrived. I jumped out almost beside myself, ran up the steps and began knocking on the door with my hands and feet. My legs, especially at the knees, had grown terribly weak. They opened quickly somehow, as though they knew I was coming. (Simonov had indeed warned them that one more might come, and here one had to give warning and take precautions in general. It was one of those “fashion shops” of those days, which have long since been wiped out by the police. By day it really was a shop; but in the evenings those who had an introduction could come as guests.) I walked quickly through the dark shop into the drawing room I knew, where only one candle was burning, and stopped in bewilderment: there was no one there.
“Where are they?” I asked someone.
But of course they had already dispersed...
Before me stood a person with a stupid smile, the madam herself, who knew me slightly. A minute later a door opened, and another person came in.

Paying no attention to anything, I paced the room and, I think, talked to myself. It was as if I had been saved from death, and I felt it joyfully with my whole being: for I would have slapped him; I would certainly, certainly have slapped him! But now they were not here, and... everything had vanished, everything had changed!.. I looked around. I could not yet take it in. Mechanically I glanced at the girl who had come in: before me flashed a fresh, young, rather pale face, with straight dark eyebrows and a serious, somewhat surprised look. I liked that at once; I would have hated her if she had smiled. I began to look at her more closely, as if with an effort: my thoughts had not yet all come together. There was something simple and kind in that face, but somehow strangely serious. I am sure that this told against her here, and none of those fools had noticed her. She could not be called a beauty, though; but she was tall, strong and well built. She was dressed extremely simply. Something nasty stung me; I went straight up to her...

I happened to look at myself in the mirror. My agitated face seemed to me utterly repulsive: pale, spiteful, mean, with dishevelled hair. “So be it; I am glad of it,” I thought. “I am glad precisely that I shall seem repulsive to her; it pleases me...”
## VI

...Somewhere behind the partition, as if under some heavy pressure, as if someone were strangling it, the clock began to wheeze. After an unnaturally long wheezing came a thin, nasty and somehow unexpectedly rapid chime, as if someone had suddenly jumped forward. It struck two. I came to myself, though I had not been asleep, only lying half-conscious.

In the narrow, cramped, low room, crowded with an enormous wardrobe and littered with cardboard boxes, rags and all sorts of old clothes, it was almost completely dark. The candle end burning on the table at the end of the room was going out altogether, now and then flaring up a little. In a few minutes there would be total darkness.

It did not take me long to come to myself; everything came back to me at once, without effort, as if it had been lying in wait for me, ready to pounce again. And even in my stupor there had remained in my memory a kind of point that would not be forgotten, around which my drowsy dreams moved heavily. But it was strange: everything that had happened to me that day seemed to me now, on waking, to have happened long, long ago, as if I had long, long since outlived it all.

My head was heavy with fumes. Something seemed to be hovering over me, brushing me, stirring me up and troubling me. Misery and bile were boiling up again and seeking an outlet. Suddenly, beside me, I saw two open eyes examining me curiously and persistently. The look was coldly indifferent, sullen, as if completely alien; it was oppressive.

A sullen thought was born in my brain and passed through my whole body like a nasty sensation, the kind you have when you go down into a cellar, damp and musty. It was somehow unnatural that only now should these two eyes have decided to begin examining me. I remembered too that for two hours I had not said a single word to this creature, and had not thought it at all necessary; earlier, for some reason, I had even liked that. But now I suddenly saw vividly the absurd idea of debauchery, disgusting as a spider: without love, crudely and shamelessly, it begins straight away with what true love is crowned by. We looked at each other like this for a long time, but she did not lower her eyes before mine and did not change her look, so that at last, for some reason, I began to feel uneasy.
“What’s your name?” I asked abruptly, to get it over with.
“Liza,” she answered almost in a whisper, but somehow quite unfriendly, and looked away.
I was silent.
“The weather today... snow... it’s foul!” I said, almost to myself, putting my hand behind my head wearily and looking at the ceiling.
She did not answer. It was all hideous.
“Are you from here?” I asked a minute later, almost angrily, turning my head a little towards her.
“No.”
“Where from?”
“From Riga,” she said reluctantly.
“German?”
“Russian.”
“Been here long?”
“Where?”
“In this house.”
“Two weeks.” She was speaking more and more abruptly. The candle had gone out completely; I could no longer make out her face.
“Have you a father and mother?”
“Yes... no... I have.”
“Where are they?”
“There... in Riga.”
“What are they?”
“Just...”
“Just what? Who are they, what class?”
“Tradespeople.”
“Did you always live with them?”
“Yes.”
“How old are you?”
“Twenty.”
“Why did you leave them?”
“Just...”
That “just” meant: leave me alone, I’m sick of it. We fell silent.

God knows why I did not go away. I myself was feeling sicker and more miserable. Images of the whole past day began to pass through my memory of their own accord, against my will, in disorder. I suddenly remembered a scene I had seen in the street that morning, as I was anxiously trotting to work.
“Today they were carrying out a coffin, and they nearly dropped it,” I suddenly said aloud, not at all wanting to start a conversation, just like that, almost by accident.
“A coffin?”
“Yes, in the Haymarket; they were carrying it up out of a cellar.”
“Out of a cellar?”
“Not a cellar, a basement... you know... down there... from a bad house... There was such filth all around... Eggshells, rubbish... it smelt... it was vile.”
Silence.
“It’s a foul day for a funeral!” I began again, just so as not to be silent.
“Why foul?”
“Snow, wet...” (I yawned.)
“It makes no difference,” she said suddenly, after a silence.
“No, it’s foul...” (I yawned again.) “The gravediggers must have been swearing because the snow was getting them wet. And there must have been water in the grave.”
“Why water in the grave?” she asked with a kind of curiosity, but speaking even more rudely and abruptly than before. Something suddenly began to egg me on.
“Why, water, at the bottom, six inches deep. You can’t dig a single dry grave at the Volkovo cemetery.”
“Why not?”
“Why not? It’s such a watery place. It’s all marsh here. So they lay them in the water. I’ve seen it myself... many times...”
