(I had not seen it even once, and had never been to the Volkovo cemetery; I had only heard people talk about it.)
“Don’t you care at all about dying?”
“Why should I die?” she answered, as if defending herself.
“You will die some day, and you will die just like that dead woman this morning. She was... a girl too... She died of consumption.”
“A tart would have died in hospital...” (She knows about that already, I thought, and she said “tart”, not “girl”.)

“She owed money to her madam,” I retorted, more and more egged on by the argument, “and she went on working for her almost to the very end, consumptive as she was. The cabmen standing around were talking to some soldiers and telling them about it. Probably her former acquaintances. They were laughing. They were even going to drink to her memory in the tavern.” (Here too I lied a great deal.)
Silence, deep silence. She did not even stir.
“And is it better to die in hospital, then?”
“Isn’t it all the same?.. And why should I die?” she added irritably.
“If not now, then later?”
“Well, later then...”
“Oh, no you don’t! Now you are young, pretty, fresh: that’s what you are valued for. But after a year of this life you won’t be the same; you’ll fade.”
“In a year?”

“In any case, in a year you’ll be worth less,” I went on gloatingly. “You’ll move from here to somewhere lower, another house. A year later, to a third, lower and lower, and in seven years or so you’ll end up in a basement in the Haymarket. And that would still be good. But the trouble will be if, on top of that, you get some illness, a weak chest, say... or catch a cold, or something. In a life like this an illness is hard to shake off. Once it takes hold, it may never let go. And so you’ll die.”
“Well, then I’ll die,” she answered, quite spitefully now, and moved quickly.
“But it’s a pity.”
“For whom?”
“A pity about life.”
Silence.
“Were you engaged to anyone? Eh?”
“What’s it to you?”
“I’m not cross-examining you. What do I care? Why are you angry? You must have had your own troubles. What’s it to me? It’s just that I’m sorry.”
“For whom?”
“Sorry for you.”
“No need...” she whispered barely audibly, and stirred again.
That at once made me angry. What! I had been so gentle with her, and she...
“What do you think, then? Are you on a good road, eh?”
“I don’t think anything.”
“That’s just what’s bad, that you don’t think. Wake up while there’s still time. And there is time. You are still young, good-looking; you could fall in love, get married, be happy...”
“Not all married women are happy,” she snapped, in her former rude patter.

“Not all, of course; but still, much better off than here. Incomparably better. And with love one can live even without happiness. Even in grief life is good; it is good to live in the world, however one lives. But here, what is there but... stench. Phew!”

I turned away in disgust; I was no longer coldly reasoning. I was beginning to feel what I was saying myself, and to grow heated. I was already longing to set out my cherished little ideas, nursed in my corner. Something suddenly caught fire in me; some aim had “appeared”.

“Don’t look at me being here; I am no example for you. I may be worse than you. I came here drunk, anyway,” I hastened to justify myself all the same. “Besides, a man is no example for a woman. It’s a different matter; though I degrade and soil myself, I am nobody’s slave: I come, I go, and I’m gone. I shake it off and I’m a different man. But you, from the very start, are a slave. Yes, a slave! You give away everything, your whole will. And later you’ll want to break these chains, but you won’t be able to: they will bind you tighter and tighter. That is the kind of accursed chain it is. I know it. I won’t even speak of other things; you wouldn’t understand, perhaps; but tell me: you must already owe your madam money? There, you see!” I added, though she had not answered, but only listened silently, with her whole being. “There’s your chain! You’ll never buy yourself out. They’ll see to that. It’s like selling your soul to the devil...

“...And besides, I... maybe I am just as unhappy, how do you know, and wallow in the mud on purpose, from misery too. People drink from grief, after all; well, and I am here from grief. Tell me, what is there good in this: here we... came together... a while ago, and we didn’t say a word to each other the whole time, and afterwards you began examining me like a wild thing, and I you. Is that how people love? Is that how one human being should come together with another? It’s simply hideous, that’s what it is!”

“Yes!” she agreed with me sharply and hastily. I was even surprised at the haste of that “yes”. So perhaps the same thought had been wandering in her head when she was examining me a while ago? So she too was capable of some thoughts?.. “Damn it, this is interesting; this is a kindred thing,” I thought, almost rubbing my hands. “And how can one fail to master such a young soul?..”
It was the game that carried me away most of all.
She turned her head closer to me and, as it seemed to me in the dark, propped it on her hand. Perhaps she was examining me. How I regretted that I could not see her eyes. I heard her deep breathing.
“Why did you come here?” I began, now with a certain authority.
“Just...”
“But how good it would be to live in your father’s house! Warm, free; your own nest.”
“And what if it was worse than this?”
“I must strike the right note,” flashed through my mind. “I won’t get far with sentimentality, perhaps.”
But it only flashed through my mind. I swear she really did interest me. Besides, I was somehow weakened and in the mood. And cunning gets on so easily with feeling.

“Who says otherwise!” I hastened to answer. “Anything can happen. I’m sure that someone wronged you, and that they are more to blame towards you than you towards them. I know nothing of your story, of course, but a girl like you surely doesn’t end up here of her own accord...”
“What sort of girl am I?” she whispered barely audibly; but I heard it.
“Damn it, I’m flattering her. That’s vile. But perhaps it’s good...” She was silent.

“You see, Liza, I’ll tell you about myself! If I had had a family since childhood, I wouldn’t be what I am now. I often think about that. However bad things are in a family, they are still your father and mother, not enemies, not strangers. Even if they show you love only once a year. All the same, you know you are at home. I grew up without a family; that must be why I turned out like this... unfeeling.”
I waited again.
“She probably doesn’t even understand,” I thought, “and it’s ridiculous anyway: moralising.”

“If I were a father and had a daughter of my own, I think I would love my daughter more than my sons, really,” I began obliquely, as if not about this at all, to distract her. I confess I was blushing.
“Why is that?” she asked.
Ah, so she’s listening!

“I don’t know, Liza. You see, I knew a father who was a stern, severe man, but he would kneel before his daughter, kiss her hands and feet, could not stop admiring her, really. She would dance at a party, and he would stand five hours in one place without taking his eyes off her. He was mad about her; I understand that. At night she would get tired and fall asleep, and he would wake up and go and kiss her and make the sign of the cross over her as she slept. He went about in a greasy old coat himself, stingy with everyone, but for her he would spend his last kopeck, give her rich presents, and it was a joy to him if she liked the present. A father always loves his daughters more than a mother does. Some girls have a happy life at home! And I think I wouldn’t even let my daughter marry.”
“Why not?” she asked, with a faint smile.

“I’d be jealous, by God. How could she kiss another man? Love a stranger more than her father? It’s painful even to imagine. Of course, it’s all nonsense; of course, everyone comes to his senses in the end. But I think that before I gave her away I would torment myself to death with worry alone: I’d reject every suitor. And I’d end up all the same by marrying her to the one she loved herself. The one the daughter loves always seems the worst of all to the father. That’s just how it is. A lot of trouble comes of it in families.”
“Some are glad to sell their daughter, never mind giving her honourably,” she said suddenly.
Ah! So that’s it!

“That, Liza, is in those accursed families where there is neither God nor love,” I took up hotly, “and where there is no love, there is no sense either. There are such families, true, but I am not talking about them. You can’t have seen any good in your family, to talk like that. You must be really unfortunate. Hm... It mostly comes from poverty.”
“And is it any better among the gentry? Honest people live well in poverty too.”

“Hm... yes. Perhaps. And there is this too, Liza: people like to count only their troubles, and do not count their happiness. If they counted it properly, they would see that every lot has its share. Well, and what if everything goes well in a family, God blesses it, the husband turns out good, loves you, cherishes you, never leaves your side! How good it is in that family! Even when it is half joy and half sorrow, it is good; and where is there no sorrow? Perhaps you’ll get married and find out yourself. But take even the first days of marriage to the man you love: what happiness, what happiness comes sometimes! And very often too. In the early days even quarrels with your husband end well. Some women, the more they love, the more quarrels they stir up with their husbands. Really; I knew one like that: ‘I love you so much, and it’s out of love that I torment you, and you should feel it.’ Do you know that one can torment a person on purpose, out of love? Women especially. And she thinks to herself: ‘But afterwards I’ll love him so much, I’ll caress him so, that it’s no sin to torment him a little now.’ And everyone in the house rejoices in you, and it is good and cheerful and peaceful and honest... Then some are jealous. He goes out somewhere (I knew one like that), and she can’t bear it, and jumps up in the middle of the night and runs out quietly to see: is he there, in that house, with that woman? That is bad. And she knows herself it is bad, and her heart sinks and torments her, but she loves him; it’s all from love. And how good it is to make up after a quarrel, to admit she was wrong, or to forgive him! And they both feel so good, it suddenly becomes so good, as if they had met anew, married anew, as if their love had begun anew. And no one, no one must know what happens between husband and wife, if they love each other. And whatever quarrel they have, they must not call even their own mother to judge between them, or tell tales about each other. They are their own judges. Love is a mystery of God and must be hidden from all strange eyes, whatever happens. It is holier for that, better. They respect each other more, and much is built on respect. And once there has been love, once they married for love, why should love pass? Can it not be kept up? It is rare that it cannot be kept up. And if the husband turns out kind and honest, how can love pass? The first married love will pass, true, but then a still better love will come. Then they will be united in soul; they will share all their affairs; they will have no secrets from each other. And when the children come, every time, even the hardest, will seem happiness; one only has to love and be brave. Then work is a joy; then one goes without bread sometimes for the children, and even that is a joy. For they will love you for it afterwards; so you are saving for yourself. The children grow, and you feel that you are an example to them, a support to them; that even when you die they will carry your feelings and thoughts all their lives, because they received them from you; they will take on your image and likeness. So it is a great duty. How can the father and mother not grow closer then? People say having children is hard. Who says so? It is heavenly happiness! Do you love little children, Liza? I love them terribly. You know: a rosy little boy at your breast, and what husband’s heart would not turn to his wife, seeing her sitting with his child! The baby, rosy and plump, sprawls and luxuriates; little arms and legs so plump, little nails so clean and tiny, so tiny it makes you laugh to look at them; little eyes as if he already understands everything. And while he sucks, he plucks at your breast with his little hand, plays with it. His father comes up, and he pulls away from the breast, bends right back, looks at his father and laughs, as if heaven knows what were so funny, and then goes back to sucking again. Or he’ll bite his mother’s breast, if his teeth are coming through, and look at her sideways with his little eyes: ‘See, I bit you!’ Isn’t it all happiness, when the three of them, husband, wife and child, are together? For such moments much can be forgiven. No, Liza, one must first learn to live oneself, and only then blame others!”

“With pictures, with pictures like these I must get at you!” I thought to myself, though, by God, I had spoken with feeling; and suddenly I blushed. “And what if she suddenly bursts out laughing; where will I hide then?” This idea drove me into a fury. Towards the end of my speech I really had grown heated, and now my vanity was somehow suffering. The silence lasted. I even wanted to nudge her.
“Why do you...” she began suddenly, and stopped.

But I had already understood everything: something different was trembling in her voice now, not sharp, not rude and unyielding as before, but something soft and shamefaced, so shamefaced that I myself suddenly felt ashamed before her, felt guilty.
“What?” I asked, with tender curiosity.
“Why, you...”
“What?”
“You... somehow... you talk just like a book,” she said, and something mocking seemed to sound in her voice again.
That remark stung me painfully. It was not what I had expected.

I did not understand that she was deliberately hiding behind mockery, that this is the usual last trick of people who are shy and chaste at heart, whose souls are being crudely and intrusively forced, and who out of pride will not give in to the last minute, and are afraid to show their feelings before you. From the very timidity with which she approached her mockery, in several attempts, and only at last brought herself to say it, I ought to have guessed. But I did not guess, and a spiteful feeling seized me.
“Just you wait,” I thought.
## VII

“Oh, come, Liza, what has a book to do with it, when I myself am sick of all this, as an outsider. And not just as an outsider. All this has woken up in my soul now... Can it be, can it be that you yourself are not sick of it here? No, habit evidently counts for a lot! The devil knows what habit can make of a person. Do you seriously think you’ll never grow old, that you’ll always be pretty, and that they’ll keep you here for ever and ever? I won’t even speak of how vile it is here... But let me tell you this, about your present life: now, although you are young, attractive, good, with a soul, with feeling; well, do you know that as soon as I came to myself just now, I at once felt sick at being here with you! One only comes here drunk. But if you were somewhere else, living as decent people live, then I might not just run after you, but simply fall in love with you; I’d be glad of a look from you, never mind a word; I’d wait for you at the gate; I’d kneel before you; I’d look at you as my bride, and think it an honour too. I wouldn’t dare think anything impure about you. But here I know that I have only to whistle, and whether you want to or not, you must come with me; and it is not I who ask your will, but you who must ask mine. The lowest peasant who hires himself out as a labourer still doesn’t sell the whole of himself into bondage, and he knows his term will come to an end. But where is your term? Just think: what are you giving away here? What are you selling into bondage? Your soul, your soul, which isn’t yours to sell, you are selling into bondage together with your body! You are giving your love to be defiled by any drunkard! Love! Why, that is everything; it is a diamond, a girl’s treasure, love! To deserve that love, a man might be ready to give his soul, to go to his death. And what is your love worth now? You are bought, all of you, entirely; and why should anyone strive for love, when everything is possible without love? Why, there is no greater insult for a girl, do you understand? I’ve heard they amuse you fools by letting you have lovers here. But that is only pampering, only deception, only a joke at your expense, and you believe it. Does he really love you, that lover? I don’t believe it. How can he love you, when he knows you can be called away from him any moment? He’s a filthy wretch, after that! Does he respect you even a drop? What have you in common with him? He laughs at you and robs you too: that’s all his love! It’s lucky if he doesn’t beat you. And perhaps he does. Ask him, if you have such a man: will he marry you? He’ll laugh in your face, if he doesn’t spit at you or hit you; and he himself, maybe, isn’t worth two broken farthings. And for what, think, have you ruined your life here? Because they give you coffee to drink and feed you well? But why do they feed you? An honest girl couldn’t swallow such a mouthful, because she’d know why she was being fed. You are in debt here, and you will always be in debt, to the very end, until the clients begin to turn up their noses at you. And that will come soon; don’t count on your youth. Here everything flies by like the mail coach. They’ll throw you out. And not simply throw you out: long before that they’ll start finding fault with you, reproaching you, abusing you, as if it were not you who gave her your health and threw away your youth and your soul for her for nothing, but as if it were you who had ruined her, beggared her, robbed her. And don’t expect support: your friends here will attack you too, to curry favour with her, because everyone here is a slave and lost conscience and pity long ago. They have sunk so low that there is no abuse on earth viler, meaner or more insulting than theirs. And you will lay down everything here, everything, without reserve: your health, your youth, your beauty, your hopes; and at twenty-two you’ll look thirty-five, and it’s lucky if you’re not ill: pray to God for that. I suppose you think now that you have no work at all, only a good time! But there is no harder, no more convict-like work in the world, and there never has been. One’s heart alone, it seems, would melt away in tears. And you won’t dare say a word, not half a word, when they drive you out of here; you’ll go as if you were the guilty one. You’ll move to another place, then a third, then somewhere else, and at last you’ll get down to the Haymarket. And there they’ll start beating you as a matter of course; that is their way of being polite there; a client there doesn’t know how to caress a girl without beating her. You don’t believe it’s so disgusting there? Go and look some day; perhaps you’ll see with your own eyes. I once saw one there, on New Year’s Day, at a door. Her own companions had thrown her out as a joke, to cool her off a little because she was howling so much, and they shut the door behind her. At nine in the morning she was already completely drunk, dishevelled, half-naked, beaten all over. Her face was powdered white, but her eyes were blackened; blood was running from her nose and her teeth: some cabman had just given her a going-over. She sat on the stone steps holding some salted fish; she was howling, wailing something about her ‘lot’, and beating the fish on the steps. And the cabmen and drunken soldiers crowded round the porch and teased her. You don’t believe you’ll be like that? I wouldn’t want to believe it either; but how do you know, perhaps ten or eight years ago this same woman with the salted fish came here from somewhere fresh as a little cherub, innocent, pure; she knew no evil; she blushed at every word. Perhaps she was just like you, proud, touchy, unlike the others; she looked like a princess and knew that perfect happiness awaited the man who would love her and whom she would love. You see how it ended? And what if at that very minute, when she was beating that fish on the dirty steps, drunk and dishevelled, what if at that minute she remembered all her former pure years in her father’s house, when she was still going to school, and the neighbour’s son waited for her on the road and swore he would love her all his life, that he would lay his destiny at her feet, and when they promised each other to love each other for ever and to marry as soon as they were grown up! No, Liza, it will be happiness, happiness for you, if you die quickly of consumption somewhere in a corner, in a cellar, like that woman this morning. In hospital, you say? All right, they’ll take you there; but what if your madam still needs you? Consumption is that kind of illness; it isn’t a fever. With it a person hopes to the last minute and says he is well. He comforts himself. And that suits the madam. Don’t worry, that’s how it is; you have sold your soul, and you owe money besides, so you won’t dare make a squeak. And when you are dying, everyone will abandon you, everyone will turn away, because what will they get out of you then? They’ll even reproach you for taking up room for nothing and not dying quickly. You’ll beg for a drink and they’ll give it to you with curses: ‘When are you going to croak, you slut? You keep us awake with your moaning; the clients don’t like it.’ That’s true; I’ve overheard such words myself. They’ll shove you, dying, into the stinkiest corner of the cellar, darkness, damp; what will you think about then, lying there alone? You’ll die, and they’ll lay you out in a hurry, strangers’ hands, grumbling, impatient; no one will bless you, no one will sigh for you; they’ll only want to get you off their hands as fast as they can. They’ll buy a coffin, carry you out as they carried out that poor woman today, and go to the tavern to drink to your memory. In the grave there’ll be slush, filth, wet snow; why should they stand on ceremony for you? ‘Let her down, Vanyukha; look at her “lot”, she’s gone in head first even here, that sort. Shorten the ropes, you rascal.’ ‘It’ll do as it is.’ ‘What do you mean, it’ll do? Look, she’s lying on her side. Was she a human being or not? Oh, well, never mind, fill it in.’ And they won’t want to quarrel over you for long. They’ll quickly shovel wet blue clay over you and go off to the tavern... And that will be the end of your memory on earth; other people have children who visit their graves, fathers, husbands; but for you, not a tear, not a sigh, not a prayer, and no one, no one, ever in the whole world will come to you; your name will vanish from the face of the earth, as if you had never been, never been born! Mud and marsh, and you may knock on the lid of your coffin at night when the dead rise: ‘Let me out, good people, to live in the world! I lived, but I never saw life; my life was used as a doormat; they drank it away in a tavern in the Haymarket; let me out, good people, to live in the world once more!..’”

I worked myself up into such pathos that a lump was rising in my own throat, and... suddenly I stopped, sat up in fright and, bending my head timidly, began to listen with a pounding heart. There was reason to be alarmed.

I had felt for a long time that I had turned her whole soul upside down and broken her heart, and the more certain I became of it, the more I wanted to reach my goal as quickly and as forcefully as possible. The game, the game carried me away; but not only the game...

I knew that I was speaking stiffly, artificially, even bookishly; in a word, I did not know how to speak except “just like a book”. But that did not trouble me; I knew, I had a feeling, that I would be understood, and that this very bookishness might help matters still more. But now, having produced the effect, I suddenly lost my nerve. No, never, never had I witnessed such despair! She lay face down, her face pressed hard into the pillow, which she clasped with both arms. Her breast was being torn apart. Her whole young body shuddered as if in convulsions. The sobs pent up in her breast choked her, tore her, and suddenly burst out in wails and cries. Then she pressed herself still harder into the pillow: she did not want anyone here, not a single living soul, to know of her torment and her tears. She bit the pillow; she bit her own hand till it bled (I saw it afterwards); or, clutching her loosened plaits with her fingers, she would go rigid with the effort, holding her breath and clenching her teeth. I began to say something to her, to beg her to calm down, but felt that I did not dare; and suddenly I myself, all in a kind of shivering fit, almost in horror, began groping about to get ready to leave, anyhow, in a hurry. It was dark: however hard I tried, I could not finish quickly. Suddenly my hand found a box of matches and a candlestick with a whole new candle. As soon as the light lit up the room, Liza suddenly sprang up, sat, and with a kind of twisted face and a half-mad smile looked at me almost senselessly. I sat down beside her and took her hands; she came to herself, rushed towards me, was about to throw her arms round me, but did not dare, and quietly bowed her head before me.
“Liza, my dear, I was wrong... forgive me,” I began, but she squeezed my hands in her fingers with such force that I realised I was saying the wrong thing, and stopped.
“Here is my address, Liza; come and see me.”
“I will...” she whispered resolutely, still not raising her head.
“And now I’ll go; goodbye... until we meet.”

I got up; she got up too, and suddenly blushed all over, shuddered, seized a shawl that lay on a chair and threw it over her shoulders right up to her chin. Having done this, she smiled again somehow painfully, blushed, and looked at me strangely. It hurt me; I hurried to leave, to vanish.

“Wait,” she said suddenly, in the passage, right by the door, stopping me with her hand on my overcoat; she hastily put down the candle and ran off; she must have remembered something, or wanted to bring something to show me. As she ran off she blushed all over; her eyes shone; a smile appeared on her lips: what could it be? I could not help waiting; she came back a minute later with a look that seemed to ask forgiveness for something. It was no longer the same face, the same look as before: sullen, mistrustful and obstinate. Her look now was pleading, soft, and at the same time trusting, tender, timid. So children look at those they love very much and of whom they are asking something. Her eyes were light hazel, beautiful eyes, lively, able to reflect both love and sullen hatred.

Without explaining anything to me, as if I, like some higher being, must know everything without explanation, she held out a piece of paper to me. Her whole face lit up at that moment with the most naive, almost childlike triumph. I unfolded it. It was a letter to her from some medical student or someone of that kind: a very high-flown, flowery, but extremely respectful declaration of love. I don’t remember the expressions now, but I remember very well that through the lofty style there showed a true feeling, which cannot be faked. When I had finished reading, I met her warm, curious and childishly impatient look fixed on me. She had riveted her eyes on my face and was impatiently waiting: what would I say? In a few words, hurriedly, but somehow joyfully and as if proudly, she explained to me that she had been at a dance somewhere, in a family house, with some “very, very good people, family people, where they know nothing yet, nothing at all”, because she was still new here and it was only for now... and she had not at all decided to stay, and would certainly leave as soon as she had paid off her debt... “Well, and that student was there; he danced with her all evening and talked to her, and it turned out that he had known her in Riga, when they were children; they had played together, only a very long time ago; and he knew her parents; but about *this* he knew nothing, nothing, nothing, and suspected nothing! And the day after the dance (three days ago) he sent her this letter through the friend she had gone to the party with... and... well, that’s all.”
She lowered her shining eyes somehow shyly when she had finished.

Poor thing, she kept that student’s letter as a treasure and had run to fetch this one treasure of hers, not wanting me to leave without knowing that she too was loved honestly and sincerely, that she too was spoken to with respect. That letter was surely destined to lie in a box with no consequences. But no matter; I am sure she would have kept it all her life as a treasure, as her pride and her justification; and now, at such a moment, she had remembered it herself and brought it, to be naively proud before me, to restore herself in my eyes, so that I too would see it, so that I too would praise it. I said nothing, pressed her hand and went out. I so wanted to leave... I walked the whole way home, although the wet snow was still falling in flakes. I was exhausted, crushed, bewildered. But the truth was already gleaming through the bewilderment. A vile truth!
## VIII

I did not soon agree to admit this truth, however. Waking the next morning after a few hours of deep, leaden sleep and at once recalling the whole of the day before, I was even amazed at my sentimentality with Liza, at all those “horrors and pities of yesterday”. “What an old woman’s fit of nerves to come over me, pah!” I decided. “And why on earth did I push my address on her? What if she comes? Oh well, let her come, perhaps; it doesn’t matter...” But obviously that was not the main and most important business now: I had to hurry and, at all costs, save my reputation in the eyes of Zverkov and Simonov as quickly as possible. That was the main business. And I even forgot about Liza altogether that morning in all my fuss.

First of all I had to repay yesterday’s debt to Simonov at once. I resolved on a desperate measure: to borrow a whole fifteen roubles from Anton Antonovich. As if on purpose, he was in the best of moods that morning and gave it to me at once, at the first request. I was so delighted at this that, signing the receipt, I told him carelessly, with a sort of dashing air, that yesterday “we had a bit of a spree with some friends at the Hôtel de Paris; we were seeing off a comrade, a childhood friend, one might even say; and, you know, he’s a great one for a spree, spoiled; of course, from a good family, a considerable fortune, a brilliant career, witty, charming, carries on affairs with certain ladies, you understand; we drank an extra ‘half dozen’ and...” And it went off fine; I said all this very easily, casually and complacently.
When I got home I immediately wrote to Simonov.

To this day I admire, remembering it, the truly gentlemanly, good-natured, frank tone of my letter. Deftly and nobly, and above all without a superfluous word, I blamed myself for everything. I excused myself, “if I may still be permitted to excuse myself”, on the grounds that, being completely unused to wine, I had got drunk on the first glass, which (I claimed) I had drunk before they came, while waiting for them at the Hôtel de Paris from five to six. I begged pardon chiefly of Simonov; and I asked him to pass on my explanations to all the others, especially Zverkov, whom, “as I remember as if in a dream”, I seem to have insulted. I added that I would have called on them all myself, but my head ached, and above all I was ashamed. I was particularly pleased with the “certain lightness”, almost carelessness (perfectly decent, though), that suddenly showed itself in my pen and, better than all possible reasons, made them understand at once that I took a rather independent view of “all that nastiness yesterday”; that I was not at all, not in the least, knocked flat, as you gentlemen probably think, but on the contrary looked at it as a calmly self-respecting gentleman should. What’s past is past, as they say; a fine fellow need not be ashamed of it.

“Why, there’s even a sort of marquis’s playfulness in it!” I admired, rereading the note. “And it all comes from being a cultured and educated man! Others in my place wouldn’t know how to get out of it, but I have wriggled out and am back on top, and all because I am ‘a cultured and educated man of our time’. And indeed, perhaps it all really did come from the wine yesterday. Hm... well, no, not from the wine. I didn’t drink any vodka at all between five and six, when I was waiting for them. I lied to Simonov; I lied shamelessly; and I’m not ashamed even now...
“But to hell with it! The main thing is that I’ve got out of it.”

I put six roubles in the letter, sealed it, and persuaded Apollon to take it to Simonov. When Apollon learned there was money in the letter, he became more respectful and agreed to go. Towards evening I went out for a walk. My head was still aching and spinning from the day before. But the more the evening came on and the thicker the dusk grew, the more my impressions changed and became confused, and my thoughts after them. Something inside me, deep in my heart and conscience, would not die, did not want to die, and showed itself in a burning anguish. I wandered mostly through the most crowded commercial streets, the Meshchanskayas, Sadovaya, by the Yusupov Garden. I always particularly liked walking along these streets at dusk, precisely when the crowd of all sorts of passers-by grows thicker there, tradesmen and workmen with faces anxious to the point of anger, going home from their day’s earnings. It was precisely this kopeck-counting bustle, this impudent prosiness, that I liked. This time all this jostling in the streets irritated me still more. I could not get control of myself, could not find the thread. Something kept rising and rising in my soul, painfully, and would not be quieted. I came home completely upset. It was as if some crime lay on my soul.

I was constantly tormented by the thought that Liza would come. What was strange to me was that of all yesterday’s memories, the memory of her tormented me in some special way, somehow quite apart from the rest. Everything else I had already managed to forget by evening; I had waved it away and was still completely satisfied with my letter to Simonov. But here I was somehow no longer satisfied. It was as if Liza alone were tormenting me. “What if she comes?” I thought ceaselessly. “Well, no matter, let her come. Hm. It’s bad enough, for one thing, that she’ll see how I live, for example. Yesterday I appeared before her as such a... hero... and now, hm! It is bad, though, that I have let myself go so much. The flat is simply squalid. And I made up my mind to go to dinner yesterday in clothes like that! And my oilcloth sofa with the stuffing sticking out! And my dressing gown that won’t close round me! What rags... And she will see all this; and she will see Apollon. That brute is sure to insult her. He’ll pick on her so as to be rude to me. And I, of course, as usual, will lose my nerve, start mincing in front of her, wrapping the skirts of my dressing gown round me, smiling, lying. Ugh, how vile! And that isn’t even the main vileness! There is something more important here, nastier, meaner! Yes, meaner! And again, again to put on that dishonest, lying mask!..”
At this thought I simply flared up:

“Why dishonest? What do you mean, dishonest? I spoke sincerely yesterday. I remember there was real feeling in me too. I wanted precisely to awaken noble feelings in her... if she cried, that is good; it will have a beneficial effect...”
But all the same I could not calm down.

All that evening, even after I had come home, even after nine o’clock, when by my reckoning Liza could not possibly come, I still kept imagining her, and, above all, I kept remembering her in one and the same position. One moment out of all of yesterday came back to me with particular vividness: when I lit up the room with the match and saw her pale, twisted face with its tormented look. And what a pitiful, what an unnatural, what a twisted smile she had at that moment! But I did not know then that fifteen years later I would still picture Liza with precisely that pitiful, twisted, useless smile she had at that moment.

The next day I was again ready to consider it all nonsense, overwrought nerves, and above all exaggeration. I was always aware of this weak spot of mine and was sometimes very afraid of it: “I exaggerate everything; that is where I limp,” I repeated to myself every hour. But all the same, “all the same, Liza will perhaps come”: that was the refrain with which all my reasoning ended in those days. I was so anxious that I sometimes flew into a rage. “She’ll come! She’s sure to come!” I exclaimed, running about the room. “If not today, then tomorrow; she’ll find me! That is the accursed romanticism of all these pure hearts! Oh, the vileness, the stupidity, the narrowness of these ‘filthy sentimental souls’! How can she not understand, how can she possibly not understand?..” But here I would stop myself, and even in great confusion.

“And how few, how few words were needed,” I thought in passing, “how little idyll was needed (and an affected, bookish, made-up idyll at that) to turn a whole human soul my way at once. That’s virginity for you! That’s freshness of soil for you!”

Sometimes the thought came to me of going to her myself, to “tell her everything” and beg her not to come to me. But at this thought such fury rose in me that I think I would have crushed that “damned” Liza if she had suddenly turned up beside me; I would have insulted her, spat at her, driven her out, struck her!

One day passed, however, a second, a third: she did not come, and I began to calm down. I felt especially encouraged and cheerful after nine o’clock; I even began sometimes to dream, and rather sweetly: “I, for example, save Liza, precisely by her coming to see me and my talking to her... I develop her, educate her. At last I notice that she loves me, loves me passionately. I pretend not to understand (I don’t know why I pretend, by the way; for effect, probably). At last, all confused, beautiful, trembling and sobbing, she throws herself at my feet and says that I am her saviour and that she loves me more than anything in the world. I am amazed, but... ‘Liza,’ I say, ‘can you really think I had not noticed your love? I saw everything, I guessed, but I did not dare to lay claim to your heart first, because I had influence over you and was afraid that, out of gratitude, you would deliberately force yourself to respond to my love, would call up in yourself a feeling that perhaps was not there; and I did not want that, because that would be... despotism... It would be indelicate’ (well, in short, here I would get carried away into some European, George-Sandish, inexpressibly noble refinement...). ‘But now, now you are mine; you are my creation; you are pure, beautiful; you are my beautiful wife.’ Then we begin to live happily ever after, go abroad, and so on and so on.” In short, I felt mean myself, and I would end by sticking my tongue out at myself.

“And they won’t let her out, the ‘hussy’!” I thought. “I don’t think they let them out walking very much, especially in the evening.” (For some reason I was certain that she must come in the evening, and at seven o’clock precisely.) “But then, she said she was not yet entirely in bondage there, that she was on a special footing; so, hm! Damn it, she’ll come; she’s sure to come!”

It was a good thing that Apollon distracted me at that time with his rudeness. He drove me past the last of my patience! He was my plague, a scourge sent upon me by Providence. We had been bickering constantly for several years on end, and I hated him. My God, how I hated him! I don’t think I have ever hated anyone in my life as I hated him, especially at certain moments. He was an elderly, dignified man who did a little tailoring on the side. But for some unknown reason he despised me, even beyond all measure, and looked down on me unbearably. However, he looked down on everyone. You had only to look at that flaxen, smoothly combed head, at the quiff he fluffed up on his forehead and greased with vegetable oil, at that solid mouth, always pursed into a little V, and you already felt before you a being who had never doubted himself. He was a pedant of the highest degree, the most enormous pedant of any I have ever met on earth; and with a vanity befitting perhaps only Alexander the Great. He was in love with every one of his buttons, every one of his fingernails: absolutely in love; he looked it! He treated me quite despotically, spoke to me extremely little, and if he happened to glance at me, he looked with a firm, majestically self-assured and constantly mocking look that sometimes drove me into a frenzy. He performed his duties with an air as if he were doing me the greatest favour. However, he did almost absolutely nothing for me, and did not even consider himself obliged to do anything. There could be no doubt that he considered me the greatest fool in the whole world, and if he “kept me on”, it was solely because he could get his wages from me every month. He agreed to “do nothing” for me for seven roubles a month. Many sins will be forgiven me on his account. At times it came to such hatred that his walk alone would almost throw me into convulsions. But what I found most loathsome of all was his lisp. His tongue was a little longer than it should be, or something of the kind, and so he constantly lisped and slobbered, and I believe he was terribly proud of it, imagining that it gave him an extraordinary amount of dignity. He spoke softly, measuredly, with his hands behind his back and his eyes on the ground. He infuriated me especially when he began reading the Psalter behind his partition. I fought many battles over that reading. But he was terribly fond of reading in the evenings, in a soft, even, sing-song voice, just as if over the dead. It is curious that that is how he ended up: he now hires himself out to read the Psalter over the dead, and also exterminates rats and makes boot polish. But in those days I could not get rid of him; it was as if he were chemically combined with my existence. Besides, he would not have agreed to leave me for anything. I could not live in furnished rooms: my flat was my private residence, my shell, my case, in which I hid from all mankind; and Apollon, the devil knows why, seemed to me to belong to this flat, and for seven whole years I could not drive him out.

To hold back his wages, for example, even for two or three days, was impossible. He would have made such a fuss that I would not have known where to hide. But in those days I was so angry with everyone that I decided, for some reason and with some purpose, to punish Apollon and not pay him his wages for another two weeks. I had long been meaning to do this, for two years or so, solely to prove to him that he must not dare to put on such airs with me, and that if I wanted to, I could always withhold his wages. I resolved not to tell him about it, and even to keep silent on purpose, so as to conquer his pride and force him to be the first to speak of his wages. Then I would take all seven roubles out of the drawer, show him that I had them and had put them aside on purpose, but that I “don’t want to, don’t want to, simply don’t want to pay him his wages; don’t want to, because that is what I want”; because such is “my will as master”; because he is disrespectful, because he is a lout; but that if he asked respectfully, I might relent and give it to him; otherwise he could wait another two weeks, three weeks, a whole month...

But however angry I was, he won all the same. I did not hold out even four days. He began as he always began in such cases, for such cases had happened before and been tried (and, I may note, I knew all this beforehand; I knew his vile tactics by heart): namely, he would begin by fixing an extremely stern look on me and not taking it off me for several minutes at a time, especially when he let me in or saw me out of the house. If, for example, I held out and pretended not to notice these looks, he would proceed, still in silence, to further tortures. Suddenly, for no reason at all, he would come quietly and smoothly into my room when I was walking about or reading, stop at the door, put one hand behind his back, set one foot forward, and fix his look on me, no longer merely stern but utterly contemptuous. If I suddenly asked him what he wanted, he would not answer, but go on staring at me for a few more seconds; then, pressing his lips together in a special way, with a significant air, he would slowly turn on the spot and slowly go back to his room. Two hours later he would suddenly come out again and appear before me in the same way. Sometimes in my fury I no longer asked him what he wanted, but simply raised my head sharply and imperiously myself and began to stare back at him. So we would stare at each other for about two minutes; at last he would turn, slowly and importantly, and go away again for two hours.

If I still did not come to my senses even then, and went on rebelling, he would suddenly begin to sigh as he looked at me, to sigh long and deeply, as if measuring with that one sigh the whole depth of my moral fall; and of course it ended at last with his winning completely: I raged and shouted, but was still forced to do what the matter was about.
This time, as soon as the usual manoeuvres of “stern looks” began, I at once lost my temper and fell on him in a fury. I was too irritated as it was.

“Stop!” I shouted in a frenzy, as he was slowly and silently turning, with one hand behind his back, to go to his room. “Stop! Come back, come back, I tell you!” And I must have bellowed so unnaturally that he turned and even began to examine me with some surprise. But he went on saying not a word, and that was what infuriated me.
“How dare you come into my room without asking and look at me like that? Answer!”
But after looking at me calmly for half a minute, he began to turn again.
“Stop!” I roared, running up to him. “Don’t move! So. Now answer: what did you come in to look at?”

“If you have anything to order me now, it is my business to carry it out,” he answered, again after a pause, softly and measuredly lisping, raising his eyebrows and calmly tilting his head from one shoulder to the other; and all this with a terrifying calm.

“That’s not what I’m asking you, not that, you executioner!” I shouted, shaking with rage. “I’ll tell you myself, executioner, why you come in here: you see that I’m not paying you your wages, you won’t bow down yourself, out of pride, to ask for them; and so you come in with your stupid looks to punish me, to torment me, and you don’t sus-s-spect, executioner, how stupid it is, stupid, stupid, stupid, stupid!”
He began to turn silently again, but I seized hold of him.

“Listen,” I shouted at him. “Here is the money, you see; here it is!” (I took it out of the table drawer.) “All seven roubles; but you won’t get it, you won’t ge-e-et it until you come respectfully, with your head bowed, and beg my pardon. Do you hear!”
“That cannot be!” he answered with a kind of unnatural self-assurance.
“It will be!” I shouted. “I give you my word of honour, it will be!”

“And there’s nothing I need to beg your pardon for,” he went on, as if not noticing my shouts at all, “because you called me an ‘executioner’, for which I can always lodge a complaint against you for insult at the police station.”

“Go! Complain!” I roared. “Go now, this minute, this second! But you are an executioner all the same! An executioner! An executioner!” But he only looked at me, then turned and, no longer listening to my shouts calling him back, went smoothly to his room without looking round.

“If it weren’t for Liza, none of this would have happened!” I decided to myself. Then, after standing for a minute, I went myself, importantly and solemnly, but with my heart beating slowly and hard, behind his screen.
“Apollon!” I said quietly and deliberately, but out of breath. “Go at once, without the least delay, and fetch the district police officer!”
He had meanwhile sat down at his table, put on his spectacles and taken up some sewing. But hearing my order, he suddenly snorted with laughter.
“Go now, this minute! Go, or you can’t imagine what will happen!”

“You really aren’t in your right mind,” he remarked, without even raising his head, lisping just as slowly and going on threading his needle. “And whoever heard of a man going to the authorities against himself? And as for frightening me, you’re only straining yourself for nothing, because nothing will happen.”
“Go!” I shrieked, seizing him by the shoulder. I felt that in a moment I would hit him.

But I did not even hear the door from the passage open quietly and slowly at that moment, and a figure come in, stop, and begin to look at us in bewilderment. I looked, nearly died of shame, and rushed into my room. There, seizing my hair with both hands, I leaned my head against the wall and froze in that position.
About two minutes later I heard Apollon’s slow steps.
“There’s some woman asking for you,” he said, looking at me particularly sternly; then he stood aside and let in... Liza. He did not want to go away, and looked at us mockingly.
“Go away! Go away!” I commanded him, losing my head. At that moment my clock strained itself, wheezed, and struck seven.
## IX

> And into my house, boldly and freely,
> come in, its mistress in full right!
— from the same poem

I stood before her crushed, disgraced, loathsomely embarrassed, and I think I was smiling, trying with all my might to wrap myself in the skirts of my shaggy, wadded old dressing gown: exactly, exactly as I had pictured it not long before, in my low spirits. Apollon stood over us for a couple of minutes and went away, but I felt no better. Worst of all, she too suddenly became embarrassed, more than I could ever have expected. Looking at me, of course.

“Sit down,” I said mechanically, and moved a chair up to the table for her, while I sat on the sofa. She sat down at once, obediently, looking at me with wide eyes and evidently expecting something from me at any moment. It was this naive expectation that drove me into a fury, but I controlled myself.
This was just the moment to try to notice nothing, as if everything were quite ordinary; but she... And I felt vaguely that she would pay dearly for all this.
“You have found me in a strange position, Liza,” I began, stammering, and knowing that this was exactly how I should not begin.

“No, no, don’t imagine anything!” I cried, seeing that she had suddenly blushed. “I am not ashamed of my poverty... On the contrary, I look on my poverty with pride. I am poor but noble... One can be poor and noble,” I muttered. “But... would you like some tea?”
“No...” she began.
“Wait!”
I jumped up and ran to Apollon. I had to vanish somewhere.

“Apollon,” I whispered in a feverish patter, throwing down in front of him the seven roubles I had been holding in my fist all along, “here are your wages; you see, I am paying you; but in return you must save me: bring tea and ten rusks from the tavern at once. If you won’t go, you will make a man unhappy! You don’t know what kind of woman this is... She is everything! You may be thinking something... But you don’t know what kind of woman this is!..”

Apollon, who had already sat down to his work and put on his spectacles again, at first, without letting go of his needle, glanced silently and sidelong at the money; then, paying no attention to me and not answering, he went on fiddling with the thread he was still threading. I waited for three minutes, standing in front of him with my arms folded *à la Napoléon*. My temples were wet with sweat; I was pale, I could feel it. But, thank God, he must have felt sorry for me, looking at me. Having finished with his thread, he slowly got up, slowly pushed back his chair, slowly took off his spectacles, slowly counted the money and at last, asking me over his shoulder whether he should get a full pot, slowly left the room. As I was going back to Liza, it occurred to me on the way: shouldn’t I just run away, as I was, in my old dressing gown, anywhere at all, and come what may?
I sat down again. She looked at me uneasily. For several minutes we were silent.
“I’ll kill him!” I cried suddenly, banging my fist on the table so hard that ink splashed out of the inkstand.
“Oh, what are you saying!” she cried, starting.
“I’ll kill him, I’ll kill him!” I shrieked, pounding the table, in a complete frenzy, and at the same time understanding completely how stupid it was to be in such a frenzy.
“You don’t know, Liza, what that executioner is to me. He is my executioner... He has gone for the rusks now; he...”
And suddenly I burst into tears. It was a fit. How ashamed I was between my sobs; but I could not hold them back. She was frightened.
“What’s the matter? What’s the matter with you?” she cried, fussing around me.

“Water, give me some water, over there!” I muttered in a weak voice, aware, however, that I could very well have done without the water and without muttering in a weak voice. But I was, as they say, putting it on, to save appearances, though the fit was real.

She gave me water, looking at me as if lost. At that moment Apollon brought in the tea. It suddenly seemed to me that this ordinary, prosaic tea was terribly indecent and paltry after everything that had happened, and I blushed. Liza looked at Apollon almost with fear. He went out without glancing at us.
“Liza, do you despise me?” I said, looking her straight in the face, trembling with impatience to know what she thought.
She was confused and did not know what to answer.

“Drink your tea!” I said spitefully. I was angry with myself, but of course it was she who had to suffer for it. A terrible spite against her suddenly boiled up in my heart; I think I could have killed her. To take revenge on her, I swore to myself not to say a single word to her the whole time. “She is the cause of it all,” I thought.

Our silence had already lasted about five minutes. The tea stood on the table; we did not touch it. I had got to the point of deliberately not wanting to begin drinking, so as to make things still harder for her; and it was awkward for her to begin. Several times she glanced at me in sad perplexity. I was stubbornly silent. The chief martyr was of course myself, because I was fully aware of all the loathsome baseness of my spiteful stupidity, and at the same time I could not restrain myself at all.

“I want to... get right away... from there,” she began, to break the silence somehow; but, poor thing! that was exactly what she should not have begun to talk about at such an already stupid moment, to such an already stupid man as me. My heart even ached with pity at her clumsiness and her needless directness. But something hideous at once crushed all the pity in me; it even egged me on still more: let the whole world go to ruin! Another five minutes passed.
“Am I in your way?” she began timidly, barely audibly, and began to get up.
But as soon as I saw this first flash of wounded dignity, I trembled with rage and at once burst out.

“Why have you come to me, will you tell me, please?” I began, gasping, and not even minding the logical order of my words. I wanted to say everything at once, in one volley; I did not even care where I began.

“Why have you come? Answer! Answer!” I cried, hardly knowing what I was doing. “I’ll tell you, my dear, why you have come. You have come because I spoke pitiful words to you that time. So you went soft, and now you want ‘pitiful words’ again. Well, know then, know that I was laughing at you that time. And I am laughing now. Why are you trembling? Yes, laughing! I had been insulted just before, at a dinner, by those men who came there before me. I came to your place to beat up one of them, the officer; but it didn’t come off, I didn’t find him; I had to take it out on someone, to get my own back; you turned up, and I vented my spite on you and laughed at you. I had been humiliated, so I wanted to humiliate; I had been ground into a rag, so I wanted to show my power... That’s what it was; and you thought I had come on purpose that time to save you, didn’t you? Is that what you thought? Is that what you thought?”

I knew that she might get confused and not understand the details; but I knew too that she would understand the essence perfectly well. And so it was. She turned white as a sheet, wanted to say something; her lips twisted painfully; but she fell on the chair as if she had been cut down with an axe. And all the time after that she listened to me with her mouth open, her eyes wide, trembling with terrible fear. The cynicism, the cynicism of my words crushed her...

“Save you!” I went on, jumping up from my chair and running back and forth in front of her about the room. “Save you from what! Why, I may be worse than you myself. Why didn’t you throw it in my face when I was preaching at you: ‘And you, what did you come here for? To read us a lesson in morals?’ Power, power was what I needed then; I needed a game; I needed to get your tears, your humiliation, your hysterics: that is what I needed then! I couldn’t bear it myself, then, because I am trash; I took fright and, the devil knows why, like a fool gave you my address. And afterwards, before I even got home, I was already cursing you for all I was worth for that address. I already hated you, because I had lied to you then. Because I only play with words, dream in my head; but in reality, do you know what I want? For you all to go to hell, that’s what! I need peace. Why, to be left undisturbed I would sell the whole world this minute for a kopeck. Is the world to go to hell, or am I to go without my tea? I say: let the world go to hell, so long as I always get my tea. Did you know that or not? Well, I know that I am a scoundrel, a wretch, an egoist, a lazybones. I have been trembling these three days for fear you would come. And do you know what worried me most these three days? That I had played such a hero before you that time, and now you would suddenly see me in this torn old dressing gown, a beggar, loathsome. I told you just now that I am not ashamed of my poverty; well, know that I am ashamed, more ashamed of it than of anything, more afraid of it than of anything, more than if I were stealing; because I am as vain as if I had been skinned, and the very air hurts me. Can it be that even now you haven’t guessed that I will never forgive you for finding me in this old dressing gown, when I was flying like a vicious little dog at Apollon? The resurrector, the former hero, flies at his servant like a mangy, shaggy mongrel, and the servant laughs at him! And the tears just now, which I could not hold back before you like a shamed old woman, I will never forgive you for! And what I am confessing to you now, I will never forgive you for either! Yes, you, you alone must answer for all this, because you turned up like that, because I am a scoundrel, because I am the nastiest, the most ridiculous, the pettiest, the stupidest, the most envious of all the worms on earth, who are not a bit better than me, but who, the devil knows why, are never embarrassed; while I will be flicked on the nose by every louse all my life: that is my trait! And what do I care if you understand nothing of this! And what, what, what do I care about you, and whether you go to ruin there or not? Do you understand how I will hate you now, having said all this to you, for having been here and listened? A man speaks out like this only once in his life, and then only in hysterics!.. What more do you want? Why, after all this, do you still stand there in front of me, tormenting me, not going away?”
But at this point a strange thing suddenly happened.

I was so used to thinking and imagining everything as in books, and picturing everything in the world as I had composed it beforehand in my dreams, that at first I did not even understand this strange thing. And what happened was this: Liza, insulted and crushed by me, understood far more than I imagined. She understood out of all this what a woman always understands first of all if she loves sincerely, namely, that I myself was unhappy.

The frightened and insulted look on her face gave way first to a sorrowful astonishment. And when I began calling myself a scoundrel and a wretch, and my tears began to flow (I spoke the whole of this tirade in tears), her whole face twitched as if in a spasm. She wanted to get up, to stop me; and when I had finished, she paid no attention to my shouts, “Why are you here, why don’t you go away!”, but to the fact that it must have been very hard for me to say all this. Besides, she was so crushed, poor thing; she thought herself infinitely beneath me; how could she be angry, or offended? She suddenly jumped up from her chair in an irresistible impulse and, straining towards me with her whole being, but still shy and not daring to move from where she stood, held out her arms to me... At that my heart too turned over. Then she suddenly rushed to me, threw her arms round my neck and began to weep. I could not hold out either, and sobbed as I had never sobbed before...

“They won’t let me... I can’t be... good!” I barely managed to say; then I went to the sofa, fell on it face down and for a quarter of an hour sobbed in real hysterics. She pressed herself to me, put her arms round me, and seemed to freeze in that embrace.

But the trouble was that the hysterics had to pass. And then (I am writing the loathsome truth) lying face down on the sofa, pressing my face hard into my wretched leather cushion, I began little by little, distantly, involuntarily but irresistibly, to feel that it would be awkward for me now to raise my head and look Liza straight in the eye. What was I ashamed of? I don’t know, but I was ashamed. It also came into my overwrought head that the roles were now completely reversed; that she was now the heroine, and I was just such a humiliated and crushed creature as she had been before me that night, four days ago... And all this came to me while I was still lying face down on the sofa!
My God! Can it be that I envied her then?

I don’t know; to this day I cannot decide; and then, of course, I could understand it even less than now. I cannot live, after all, without power and tyranny over someone... But... but nothing can be explained by reasoning, and consequently there is no point in reasoning.

I overcame myself, however, and raised my head: I had to raise it some time... And I am convinced to this day that precisely because I was ashamed to look at her, another feeling suddenly kindled and flared up in my heart then... a feeling of mastery and possession. My eyes gleamed with passion, and I gripped her hands hard. How I hated her, and how drawn to her I was at that moment! One feeling strengthened the other. It was almost like revenge!.. On her face there appeared at first a kind of bewilderment, even fear, but only for a moment. She embraced me rapturously and warmly.

A quarter of an hour later I was running back and forth about the room in furious impatience, every minute going up to the screen and peeping through the crack at Liza. She was sitting on the floor with her head leaning against the bed, and must have been crying. But she did not go away, and that was what irritated me. This time she knew everything. I had insulted her finally, but... there is no need to tell it. She had guessed that the outburst of my passion was precisely revenge, a new humiliation for her, and that to my earlier, almost objectless hatred there was now added a personal, envious hatred of her... However, I don’t claim that she understood all this clearly; but she did understand fully that I was a vile man and, above all, incapable of loving her.

I know I shall be told that this is incredible, that it is incredible to be as spiteful and stupid as I was; perhaps they will add that it was incredible not to love her, or at least not to value that love. Why incredible? In the first place, I could no longer love, because, I repeat, to love meant for me to tyrannise and to be morally superior. All my life I could not even imagine any other love, and I have come to the point that I sometimes think now that love consists precisely in the right, voluntarily given by the beloved, to tyrannise over her. Even in my underground dreams I never imagined love except as a struggle; I always began it with hatred and ended it with moral subjugation, and afterwards I could not even imagine what to do with the subjugated object. And what is incredible in it, when I had already managed to corrupt myself morally so far, had become so unused to “living life”, that just now I had thought of reproaching her and shaming her for having come to me to hear “pitiful words”; and I had not guessed myself that she had come not at all to hear pitiful words, but to love me, because for a woman it is in love that all resurrection lies, all salvation from any ruin whatever, and all rebirth; and it cannot show itself in any other way. However, I did not hate her so very much when I was running about the room and peeping through the crack behind the screen. It was only unbearably hard for me that she was here. I wanted her to vanish. I wanted “peace”; I wanted to be left alone in the underground. “Living life”, which I was not used to, had crushed me so that it was even hard to breathe.

But several more minutes passed, and still she did not get up, as if she were unconscious. I had the shamelessness to knock softly on the screen to remind her... She suddenly started, jumped up, and rushed to look for her shawl, her hat, her coat, as if escaping from me somewhere... Two minutes later she came slowly out from behind the screen and looked at me heavily. I grinned spitefully, but forcibly, for appearance’s sake, and turned away from her look.
“Goodbye,” she said, going towards the door.
I suddenly ran up to her, seized her hand, opened it, put something in it... and closed it again. Then at once I turned away and sprang quickly into the other corner, so as at least not to see...

I wanted to lie just now, to write that I did this accidentally, beside myself, at a loss, foolishly. But I don’t want to lie, and so I say straight out that I opened her hand and put that in it... out of spite. It occurred to me to do it while I was running back and forth about the room and she was sitting behind the screen. But this I can say for certain: I did this cruel thing, though on purpose, not from my heart but from my wretched head. This cruelty was so put-on, so cerebral, so deliberately invented, so bookish, that I could not bear it myself even for a minute: first I sprang into the corner so as not to see, and then in shame and despair I rushed after Liza. I opened the door to the passage and began to listen.
“Liza! Liza!” I called down the stairs, but timidly, in an undertone...
There was no answer; I thought I heard her steps on the bottom stairs.
“Liza!” I called louder.
No answer. But at that very moment I heard from below the stiff glass outer door to the street open heavily, with a screech, and slam stiffly shut. The boom rose up the stairs.
She had gone. I went back into the room, deep in thought. I felt terribly heavy.

I stopped by the table, next to the chair on which she had sat, and stared senselessly in front of me. About a minute passed; suddenly I started all over: right in front of me, on the table, I saw... in a word, I saw a crumpled blue five-rouble note, the very one I had pressed into her hand a minute before. It was that note; it could not have been any other; there was no other in the house. So she had managed to throw it from her hand onto the table at the moment when I sprang into the other corner.

Well? I might have expected her to do that. Might have expected it? No. I was such an egoist, I respected people so little in reality, that I could not even imagine that she would do it. That I could not bear. A moment later, like a madman, I rushed to dress, threw on whatever I could in my haste, and ran out headlong after her. She could not have gone two hundred paces when I ran out into the street.

It was quiet; the snow was falling thickly, almost straight down, laying a cushion on the pavement and the empty street. There were no passers-by; not a sound could be heard. The street lamps flickered gloomily and uselessly. I ran some two hundred paces to the crossroads and stopped.

“Where did she go? And why am I running after her? Why? To fall down before her, to sob with remorse, to kiss her feet, to beg for forgiveness! I did want that; my whole breast was being torn to pieces, and never, never shall I remember that moment with indifference. But why?” I thought. “Won’t I hate her, perhaps tomorrow, precisely because I kissed her feet today? Will I give her happiness? Haven’t I learned again today, for the hundredth time, what I am worth? Won’t I torment her to death?”
I stood in the snow, peering into the murky haze, and thought about this.

“And won’t it be better, won’t it be better,” I fantasised afterwards at home, drowning the living pain in my heart with fantasies, “won’t it be better if she carries away the insult with her now for ever? An insult: why, that is purification; it is the most stinging and painful consciousness! Tomorrow I would have soiled her soul with myself and worn out her heart. But now the insult will never die in her; and however vile the filth that awaits her, the insult will raise her up and purify her... by hatred... hm... perhaps by forgiveness too... But will it all make things any easier for her?”
And really: here I am now asking an idle question of my own: which is better, cheap happiness or exalted suffering? Well, which is better?

So I dreamed as I sat at home that evening, barely alive with the pain in my soul. Never had I endured so much suffering and remorse; but could there have been the slightest doubt, when I ran out of the flat, that I would turn back home halfway? I never met Liza again, and heard nothing of her. I will add, too, that for a long time I remained pleased with my phrase about the usefulness of insult and hatred, although I nearly fell ill from misery at the time.

Even now, after so many years, all this comes back to me somehow too painfully. Much comes back to me painfully now, but... hadn’t I better end my “Notes” here? I think I made a mistake in beginning to write them. At least I have been ashamed all the while I was writing this story: so it is no longer literature but a corrective punishment. For to tell long stories, for example, about how I failed in my life through moral corruption in a corner, through the lack of proper surroundings, through being cut off from living life, and through vain spite in the underground: by God, it is not interesting. A novel needs a hero, and here all the traits of an anti-hero have been collected on purpose; and above all, all this will make a most unpleasant impression, because we have all lost touch with life, we are all lame, every one of us, more or less. We have lost touch with it so much that we sometimes feel a kind of loathing for real “living life”, and so we cannot bear to be reminded of it. Why, we have come to the point of almost regarding real “living life” as hard work, almost as a job, and we all agree in private that it is better in books. And why do we sometimes fuss about, why do we carry on, what are we asking for? We don’t know ourselves. It would be worse for us if our whimsical requests were granted. Go on, try: give us, for example, a little more independence, untie the hands of any one of us, widen our sphere of activity, relax the supervision, and we... why, I assure you, we would at once ask to be taken back under supervision. I know you will perhaps be angry with me for this, shout and stamp your feet: “Speak for yourself alone and your miseries in the underground, but don’t you dare say ‘all of us’!” Excuse me, gentlemen; I am not justifying myself with this “all of us”. As for me in particular, I have only carried to an extreme in my life what you have not dared to carry even halfway; and you have taken your cowardice for good sense, and found comfort in that, deceiving yourselves. So that perhaps I am even more “alive” than you. Look more closely! Why, we don’t even know where living life lives now, or what it is, or what it is called. Leave us alone, without books, and we shall at once get confused and lost; we shall not know what to join, what to hold on to, what to love and what to hate, what to respect and what to despise. We find it a burden even to be human beings, human beings with our own real bodies and blood; we are ashamed of it, we think it a disgrace, and we try to be some sort of never-existing generalised humans. We are stillborn, and for a long time now we have been born not of living fathers, and we like this more and more. We are acquiring a taste for it. Soon we shall invent a way of being born somehow from an idea. But enough; I don’t want to write any more “from the Underground”...
However, the “notes” of this paradoxalist do not end here. He could not resist, and went on. But it seems to us too that this is a good place to stop.
